Locating missing children and elderly individuals or others that are vulnerable/endangered, including those associated with AMBER, Silver, and Missing Indigenous Person Alerts.

Locating vehicles that are stolen, wanted, or subject of a criminal investigation.

Locating witnesses and victims of violent crimes.

Operating PTZ cameras in real-time for active monitoring or adjusting to focus on specific areas of interest if there is specific information that a reasonable officer construes as a threat to community safety or a lifesaving effort.

Purposes related to training Flock Safety Camera users.
Supporting local, state, federal, and tribal community safety departments in the identification of vehicles and/or persons associated with criminal investigations, including investigations of serial crimes.

Utilizing PTZ Cameras to observe public locations during a critical incident to improve situational awareness for responding officers.

everett-wa-pd:
All employees of the Everett Police Department, including commissioned officers and civilian personnel, shall abide by the policies and procedures related to Flock Safety Cameras as set forth in this policy. Employees of the police department are prohibited from using Flock Safety Camera technology in the following circumstances:

Employees may not use Flock Safety Cameras for non-work-related purposes or otherwise operate the Flock Safety Cameras outside their legitimate law enforcement duties.

Flock Safety Cameras may be used to collect data that is within public view but will not be used for the sole purpose of monitoring individual or expressive activities protected by the First Amendment of the United States Constitution.

Flock Safety Cameras shall not be used solely for the purpose of immigration enforcement.

Flock Safety Cameras shall not be used to investigate or issue infractions.

In no case shall the Everett Police Department's Flock Safety Cameras be used for any purpose other than legitimate law enforcement or community safety purposes.

The use of Flock Safety cameras should avoid any conflicts of interest as prescribed in EPD Policy 4.50.

Users will not target any person based on their actual or perceived age, color, creed, criminal history, disability, ethnic background, gender, gender expression or identity, lifestyle, marital status, national origin, partnership status, political affiliation or beliefs, pregnancy status, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation as defined by RCW 49.60.040, social or economic status, veteran status, and, to the extent permitted by law, alienage or citizenship status, or any other legally protected status.

Without another clearly articulated nexus to criminal activity associated with Washington State law, Flock Safety Cameras shall not be used to specifically target or track the movement of vehicles traveling to or from healthcare facilities, including, but not limited to hospitals, clinics, mental health providers, or reproductive health care centers. This restriction applies irrespective of the vehicle's origin, destination, or the medical services sought by the individuals.

lynnwood-wa-pd:
All employees of the Lynnwood Police Department, including commissioned officers and civilian personnel, shall abide by the policies and procedures related to Flock Safety Cameras as set forth in this policy. Employees of the police department are prohibited from using Flock Safety Camera technology in the following circumstances:

Employees may not use Flock Safety Cameras for non-work-related purposes or otherwise operate the Flock Safety Cameras outside their legitimate law enforcement duties.

Flock Safety Cameras may be used to collect data that is within public view but will not be used for the sole purpose of monitoring individual or expressive activities protected by the First Amendment of the United States Constitution.

Flock Safety Cameras shall not be used solely for the purpose of immigration enforcement.

Flock Safety Cameras shall not be used to investigate or issue infractions.

In no case shall the Lynnwood Police Department's Flock Safety Cameras be used for any purpose other than legitimate law enforcement or community safety purposes.

Users will not target any person based on their actual or perceived age, color, creed, criminal history, disability, ethnic background, gender, gender expression or identity, lifestyle, marital status, national origin, partnership status, political affiliation or beliefs, pregnancy status, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation as defined by RCW 49.60.040, social or economic status, veteran status, and, to the extent permitted by law, alienage or citizenship status, or any other legally protected status.

Without another clearly articulated nexus to criminal activity associated with Washington State law, Flock Safety Cameras shall not be used to specifically target or track the movement of vehicles traveling to or from healthcare facilities, including, but not limited to hospitals, clinics, mental health providers, or reproductive health care centers. This restriction applies irrespective of the vehicle's origin, destination, or the medical services sought by the individuals.

-el-cajon-pd-ca:
On October 28, 2023, at approximately 11:57 PM, the El Cajon Police Department responded to multiple 9-1-1 calls reporting a large house party and gunshots in the 700 block of Mahogany Drive in El Cajon, California. Officers arrived to find numerous individuals fleeing the area and located two victimsa 16-year-old male and an 18-year-old malesuffering from critical gunshot wounds. Both victims later died after being transported to local trauma hospitals.

Homicide detectives determined that at least two suspects fled the scene in a vehicle prior to police arrival. Investigators used the citys Flock Safety automated license plate reader cameras to identify the suspected getaway vehicle, which led to the identification of two suspects from San Diego.

One suspect was later taken into custody by the Chula Vista Police Department on November 18 during an unrelated firearm arrest. On November 20, officers and detectives from the El Cajon Police Department, with assistance from the United States Marshals Service Fugitive Task Force and the East County Regional Gang Task Force, located and arrested the second suspect in San Diego, bringing the homicide investigation closer to resolution.

Sex offender arrested after alleged lewd act in public and flashing a fake firearm in Marina

MARINA, Calif. (KION-TV)- Marina Police said a man was arrested after allegedly committing a lewd act in public in front of a business along the 200 block of Reservation Road over the weekend. This all happened around 8:17 p.m. on Sunday. Police said the victim's boyfriend confronted the suspect and the suspect flashed what looked like a firearm. The boyfriend backed away and the police were called. The suspect, later identified as Joseph Connor, 61, of Fairfield, left the scene. Police said they obtained photos of the suspect and his vehicle. The vehicle was then spotted the following morning by a Salinas Police FLOCK camera. Salinas Police then found Connors on the 700 block of East Street at around 11:15 a.m.

Marina Police arrived after Connors was detained. A search of his vehicle revealed an imitation firearm, said police. The suspect was booked into Monterey County Jail for lewd acts in public and exhibiting an imitation firearm, said police.

piedmont-ca-pd:
On 01/07/2026 at approximately 1647 hours, Piedmont Police Officers were dispatched to a report of a tool theft in progress. Upon our quick response, it was determined that unknown suspect(s) had just stolen a 2026 GMC Sierra 3500HD along with an attached dump trailer hauling a large quantity of concrete. The suspect(s) fled the scene in the stolen vehicle and trailer but lost control several blocks away due to the weight, ultimately colliding with a residence.

Using nearby surveillance cameras, we observed a suspect vehicle, a dark colored Honda Accord, associated with the theft of the GMC. Through Flock ALPR technology, I initially captured only a side profile image of the suspect vehicle as it fled out of town. I submitted a request for additional footage from one of our Flock cameras and was able to review the footage frame by frame. This allowed me to obtain a partial rear license plate; while four characters were obstructed, the last three characters were visible.

Using the vehicle description, visible stickers, and the last three characters of the plate, I searched 30 days of history for similar vehicles ending in #310. This led to the identification of the suspect vehicles full license plate and a possible suspect believed to be related to or associated with the registered owner.

The case is still ongoing, but thanks to Flock ALPR technology, we now have strong, reliable leads that are significantly advancing the investigation.

accomack-county-va-so:
POLICY & PROCEDURES SECTION: ADMINISTRATION GENERAL ORDER: 024.3
SUBJECT:
EFFECTIVE DATE: 07/01/2025
AUTOMATED LICENSE PLATE SUPERSEDES:
RECOGNITION (ALPR) SYSTEM ISSUED BY: WTW
ACCREDITATION STANDARD: (NOT REQUIRED)

I. PURPOSE
This policy establishes guidelines for the proper use, management, and oversight of the Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) system utilized by the Accomack County Sheriffs Office (ACSO). This policy ensures compliance with Virginia Code � 2.2-5517 and � 52-30.2, while also reflecting best practices from peer agencies to ensure operational integrity, transparency, and respect for individual privacy.

II. POLICY
The ACSO shall use ALPR systems exclusively for official law enforcement purposes. These include locating stolen vehicles, missing persons, wanted individuals, and vehicles associated with criminal investigations or alerts such as AMBER, SILVER, and BOLO notices. All ALPR searches or alerts initiated for criminal investigations must be based on reasonable suspicion, as required by � 2.2-5517(D). Misuse of ALPR equipment or data will result in disciplinary action and may include criminal or civil penalties. An ALPR alert alone does not constitute probable cause.

ALPR data shall not be shared with law enforcement agencies outside of Virginia, consistent with Code � 2.2-5517.

All ALPR vendor contracts shall comply with VA Code � 2.2-5517 and include clauses ensuring data ownership by the agency, audit capabilities, secure deletion, and immediate notification upon receipt of legal process for data.

This policy shall be reviewed annually to ensure ongoing compliance with applicable law and technological updates.

III. DEFINITIONS
" ALPR System: Camera and software technology that captures and converts license plate images into readable data.
" System Data: Metadata associated with license plate captures (e.g., date, time, location).
" Audit Trail: All records of queries and responses in an automatic license plate recognition system, and all records of actions in which system data is accessed, entered, updated, shared, or disseminated. This includes:
(i) Date and time of access;
(ii) License plate number or other data elements used to query the system;
(iii) Specific purpose for accessing or querying the system, including offense type;
(iv) Associated call for service or case number;
(v) Username of the person who accessed or queried the system.
" Hit: A system alert indicating a possible match between a captured plate and a hot list entry.
" Hot List: Databases containing plates associated with criminal activity, missing persons, or other law enforcement interest.
" Custom Hot List: Manually created entries by ACSO personnel for investigative purposes.
" ALPR Administrator: The Lieutenant of Criminal Investigations or their designee.

IV. SYSTEM ACCESS AND USER ACCOUNTABILITY
1. All users must:
o Hold current VCIN certification.
o Complete ALPR vendor-approved training.
o Log into the ALPR system at the beginning of each shift.
2. All queries and access must:
o Include a case number or search reason.
o Be auditable.
o Have the outcome section completed at the completion of the search investigation. Failure to complete the outcome section will result in revocation of access privileges.
3. Users are assigned access based on their role and responsibilities.

V. HIT VERIFICATION AND RESPONSE
1. Upon receiving a hit, officers must:
o Visually verify the plate and vehicle characteristics.
o Contact Accomack County Sheriffs Office Communications Deputy (Dispatch) for VCIN/NCIC confirmation.
o Determine whether the alert pertains to a stolen plate, stolen vehicle, wanted subject, etc.
o Avoid taking enforcement action solely based on an ALPR alert.
2. Additional steps:
o Accomack County Sheriffs Office Communications Deputy (Dispatch) must verify violent gang member or terrorist watch list alerts.
o Officers must treat these alerts as intelligence only, not grounds for a stop.

VI. HOT LIST MANAGEMENT
1. The ALPR system automatically updates hot lists from NCIC/VCIN daily.
2. Supervisors must approve custom hot list entries.
3. Investigating officers must request timely removal of irrelevant entries.
4. The ALPR Administrator shall:
o Conduct monthly reviews of custom hot lists.
o Ensure only relevant and active investigations are supported.

VII. DATA STORAGE AND RETENTION
1. System Data:
o Purged automatically after 21 days, unless retained for evidentiary or investigative purposes.
2. Audit Trail Data:
o Retained for 2 years.
3. Evidentiary Data:
o Stored per Library of Virginias GS-17 schedule.
o Must be transferred to evidence storage systems.
4. Prohibited Actions:
o No manual downloading or saving unless approved.
o No personal use or secondary dissemination of ALPR data.

VIII. DATA SHARING AND SECURITY
1. ALPR data shall not be:
o Sold, exchanged, or shared for non-law enforcement purposes.
o Shared with ICE, CBP, or other immigration enforcement entities.
2. Data may be shared:
o With other law enforcement agencies for valid purposes (within Virginia).
o With the Commonwealths Attorney for prosecution.
o Via court order, subpoena, or FOIA exemption compliance.
o With vendors (e.g., Flock Safety) strictly for maintenance.
3. The ALPR Administrator manages sharing permissions and vendor access.

IX. AUDITING AND COMPLIANCE
1. The ALPR Administrator shall:
o Audit system usage monthly.
o Submit quarterly compliance reports to the Sheriff.
o Identify misuse, errors, and correct policy deviations.
2. All audits must include:
o Hot list entries/reviews.
o User activity.
o System alerts and outcomes.

X. REPORTING AND PUBLIC AWARENESS
1. Required Annual Report (due April 1):
o Total ALPR cameras by type and location.
o Number and reasons for system queries.
o Demographics of individuals affected by stops.
o Instances of unauthorized access.
2. Public Posting:
o This policy and the annual report must be posted publicly, redacting any sensitive data.
o Public awareness campaign to commence by September 1, 2025.

XI. TRAINING
1. All users must complete:
o Initial vendor-approved training.
o Annual refresher training.
o VCIN certification and recertification.
2. Training:
o The ALPR Administrator shall maintain all training records.
o Division Supervisors should coordinate, monthly, with the ALPR Administrator to ensure user compliance.

XII. VIOLATIONS AND ENFORCEMENT
1. Misuse of ALPR systems or data will result in disciplinary action.
2. Any evidence obtained in violation of this policy may be deemed inadmissible.
3. Violations may result in:
o Criminal charges under Virginia law.
o Civil liability.
o Administrative sanctions.

auburn-wa-pd:
In the spring of 2025, Auburn Police responded to a call for service which resulted in a homicide investigation. During the investigation, APD personnel learned that a specific vehicle was used by the suspects to flee the scene. Using city owned camera footage, APD personnel managed to obtain some video of the suspect vehicle, but the clarity was limited, only allowing APD personnel to gather a general description of its make and model.

However, when APD personnel searched the Flock Safety Camera system in our city, a matching make and model was quickly located, which provided APD with a license plate number. By combining the information from the city owned camera systems with Flock, APD personnel were able to confirm the exact vehicle involved in the homicide. Within six hours, APD personnel entered the license plate into a WA State system as a Be On the Look Out (BOLO) for the awareness of all law enforcement.

Later that day, an officer from an outside agency found the suspect vehicle abandoned on the side of the road. Thanks to the quick identification of the vehicle, APD personnel were able to collect very valuable evidence. This success would not have been possible without Flock. The suspect in the homicide was later arrested and booked into jail.
augusta-county-va-so: On December 7, 2024, the Augusta County Sheriff's Office received HIT text messages for a stolen vehicle that drove past one of our Flock cameras. Deputies canvassed the area for the next few hours and were able to locate the stolen vehicle from another jurisdiction at one of our local motels. The vehicle was recovered and the suspect was arrested.
barrow-county-ga-so:
On April 24, 2024, A Criminal Investigations Lieutenant was on their way to work when they received a Hotlist hit in reference to a missing elderly female. The elderly female had been missing since 6 PM of the previous day. The lieutenant noticed that the vehicle was in front of them. They activated their emergency lights and conducted a traffic stop on the vehicle. The lieutenant approached the vehicle and contacted the driver an elderly female. The female did not know where she was. She stated she was trying to get back to Walton County but did not know how to get there. The lieutenant was able to contact a family member and was able to reconnect the elderly female back with her family.

Using Flock Safety, the Barrow County Sheriffs Office was able to help someone in need of help return home to their family. Who knows what would have happened if there were no Flock Safety cameras in the county.
caldwell-id-pd-: On 1-1-26, our Real Time Crime Center utilized Flock ALPR and traffic camera technology to identify a suspect vehicle within 10 minutes after it was involved in an armed robbery. The vehicle was later identified at a residence and a subsequent search warrant and follow up yielded a confession and the recovery of the stolen property taken during the robbery. Due to the quick identification of suspects and vehicle, evidence was recovered in this case that would normally have been lost. Due to the license plate reader and live-stream video technology deployed in the City of Caldwell, only one enforcement stop was made during the follow up investigation. When compared to traditional policing practices, technology helped the police reduce unnecessary contact with the public by strategically focusing on those offenders directly linked to the crime. Essentially shrinking the policing impact on our community.
chula-vista-ca-pd:
On January 11, 2026 Chula Vista PD officers responded to a hit-and-run collision near the intersection of North Greensview Dr. and Park Meadows Rd., where an elderly female pedestrian was found critically injured in the roadway. The driver fled the scene before authorities arrived, and the victim later died at a hospital from her injuries. With very limited suspect information, investigators canvassed the area, interviewed residents, and searched for video evidence. With the limited vehicle description the detectives developed, they turned to Flock where they successfully found the vehicle and license plate. On January 13, 2026, the technology led them to a residence in the city, where they identified and arrested a female suspect believed to be the driver. The suspect is being charged with felony hit-and-run and misdemeanor vehicular manslaughter.

franklin-ma-pd: Flock plate readers operated by the Franklin Police were able to identify a vehicle involved with numerous business break-ins. The vehicle was located through the use of the Flock information search network and recovered in Rhode Island. After recovery, the vehicle was determined to be a stolen vehicle from the Boston area. lakewood-wa-pd:
In the summer of 2024, Lakewood Police responded to a call for service which resulted in a homicide investigation. During the investigation, LPD personnel learned that a specific vehicle was used by the suspects to flee the scene from witnesses on scene. Unfortunately, no plate information was available, and the neighboring businesses surveillance clarity was limited to description of its make and model. However, when LPD personnel searched the Flock Safety Camera system in our city, a matching make and model was quickly located leaving the scene when the homicide occurred. This provided LPD with a license plate number.

By combining this information with other information obtained through warrants, LPD personnel were able to confirm the exact vehicle involved in the homicide. By identifying the vehicle early in the investigation, other surveillance videos were able to be located and helped to identify the suspects involved. This success would not have been possible without Flock. The suspects in the homicide were later arrested and booked into jail.
loveland-oh-pd:
On December 1, 2024, LPD received a report of a Breaking and Entering offense at a downtown business. The only lead was a general time frame and a video image of a hooded suspect inside the establishment.

Utilizing the FLOCK database, officers worked to establish a list of vehicles in the area around the time of the offense. Their efforts produced a list of approximately 32 vehicles including one related to a previous employee. When interviewed the suspect admitted to multiple offenses.

The FLOCK information saved numerous investigative hours and enhanced the officer's ability to advance the investigation much faster than if forced to review hours of surveillance footage.
miami-township-oh-pd-clermont:
A Miami Township officer on patrol received a Flock alert for a stolen vehicle. The officer stopped the vehicle. Two handguns and narcotics were recovered. Two suspects were arrested.

Miami Township officers responded to an assisted living facility for a van that was stolen. A Flock camera showed the van entering Lowe's parking lot in Miami Township shortly after the theft. The suspect was seen on surveillance video leaving Lowe's with items he purchased and walking back to the stolen van. Subsequently, the suspect was arrested later that evening at Miami Valley Gaming by Warren County Deputies and was found in possession of the keys to the stolen van. The suspect was charged with Theft of a Motor Vehicle.

Miami Township officers responded to a local business for a theft of a trailer. Surveillance footage was available at the scene that showed the suspect in his vehicle committing the offense. Utilizing Flock cameras, detectives were able to locate the suspects vehicle. This generated a lead that allowed officers to execute a search warrant at the suspects residence where evidence of the crime was located. The suspect was charged with Theft.

Several firearms were reported stolen from a pawn shop in Miami Township. A suspect was named in the case. During the investigation, detectives were able to locate the suspects vehicle on Flock cameras in the Dayton area shortly after the offense occurred. A check of Dayton pawn shops resulted in one of the firearms being recovered. The suspect was interviewed and was eventually arrested for the theft of the firearms.
minerva-park-oh-pd:
1. In October, 2021 a man approached a resident and asked to borrow a shovel. While the resident was getting the shovel, the man entered the home and stole the residents wallet and cell phone. The man then got into a black four-door car and left the area without the shovel. Later, the man discovered the missing phone and wallet and reported the theft to Minerva Park Police.

Using the Flock camera system, officers were able to search for a black car near the time of the incident. They were able to identify a vehicle and through the owner of the vehicle, a suspect. The suspect was arrested for Burglary and Theft. The residents property was returned.

2. In the summer of 2022, a series of mail thefts occurred in the village. After a few incidents, a residents security video captured a description of an older model pickup truck with distinctive stickers on the rear of the truck cap. Searching through Flock cameras and extending the search to neighboring departments Flock cameras, Minerva Park Police were able to identify the truck and get a plate number. The vehicle owner no longer lived at the address registered to the vehicle, but an officer spotted the suspect vehicle a few days later in the village. The suspect vehicle was stopped and stolen mail was discovered in the vehicle. Both the vehicle owner and a passenger were charged with several counts of mail theft.

3. In July of 2024 a vehicle pulled into the lot of the middle school and using airsoft type weapons fired projectiles into a group of students attending summer school. Flock was used to find the vehicle entering the village and a license plate was obtained. A search of the license plate revealed the suspects had spray painted the vehicle a different color within hours of the incident. The vehicle was located and several juvenile suspects were charged and referred to Juvenile Court.
monona-wi-pd: The Flock system was key in locating a suspect of an ongoing and very dangerous stalking case. The suspect stalked the victim on multiple occasions after going on a date. The individual was arrested by MOPD and later released on bail. Days later, the system alerted MOPD that the offenders vehicle had returned to the area, despite a court order to remain out of Dane County. The information was verified, and the suspect was stopped and arrested. Probable cause was established to make an arrest. Investigators believed that the suspect was on their way to the victims residence in Monona.
nd-west-fargo-pd:
At approximately 3 a.m. Tuesday, July 1, 2025, the West Fargo Police Department attempted to stop a vehicle near the intersection of 7th Avenue and 9th Street E. for a traffic violation. The driver of the vehicle fled after law enforcement attempted the traffic stop and a pursuit was initiated. The suspect fled eastbound towards the City of Fargo, causing officers to terminate the pursuit.

At approximately 10:45 p.m. Tuesday, July 1, the West Fargo Police Department received a Flock Safety Camera System notification that the suspect vehicle had been located within the City of Fargo. West Fargo Police Department officers successfully located and apprehended the suspect vehicle near the intersection of 45th Street and 13th Avenue S.

The driver, from Horace, ND, was arrested for felony fleeing in a motor vehicle, felony possession of methamphetamine, felony possession of methadone, possession of drug paraphernalia, driving under suspension, and an outstanding warrant.

There were no injuries to emergency personnel, suspects or bystanders. The suspect vehicle was impounded.
north-liberty-ia-pd: Officers used Flock to obtain the license plate of a vehicle that fled the scene of a personal injury accident. In less than ten minutes, officers were able to locate the vehicle and identify the driver, who has been charged in relation to the collision.
northglenn-co-pd:
On December 22nd, 2025, a Flock alert helped officers quickly locate a stolen U-Haul at the Northglenn Marketplace. Using nearby surveillance and coordinated response, officers identified the suspect associated with the vehicle. The stolen vehicle was recovered, a suspect was taken into custody, and additional drugs and stolen items were recovered, preventing further criminal activity and vehicle damage.

On November 14th, 2025, Law enforcement agencies received information indicating an individual in crisis had made credible threats of self-harm and potential harm to others while driving throughout the metro area. Officers identified the vehicle and immediately issued a metro-wide BOLO using Flock Safety. Within minutes, Flock cameras alerted officers to the vehicles location near a major interstate and again in a nearby residential area. These real-time alerts allowed officers to quickly locate and safely stop the vehicle before the situation escalated. The individual was taken into protective custody and transported for a mental health evaluation. The timely Flock hit played a critical role in preventing possible self-harm or harm to others.

On June 1st, 2025, officers were dispatched to a cold hit-and-run involving a parked vehicle. Officers found a car piece on scene. They checked the part number on scene and determined it belonged to a Cadillac sedan. Nearby Flock cameras were checked, and a Cadillac was spotted driving in the area right before the collision. Officers went to the registered owners address and found the vehicle in the driveway. It had extensive damage that lined up with the collision they were investigating.

On May 31st, 2025, officers were alerted through a Flock automated license plate reader to a stolen Kia Soul entering the Marketplace. Officers investigating the stolen vehicle observed the vehicle parked outside an open business. Officers formulated a plan and began conducting surveillance on the vehicle. A male suspect exited the store and attempted to enter the stolen vehicle. Officers attempted to contact the suspect when the suspect fled on foot. During the chase, the suspect approached a running vehicle, threatened the driver with a screwdriver, and forcibly attempted to steal the vehicle. A pursuing officer was able to intervene in the vehicular hijacking and take the suspect into custody after multiple taser deployments. The suspect was booked on felony charges, including attempted carjacking, motor vehicle theft and felony menacing.

On May 21st, 2025, officers received a Flock camera alert for a vehicle connected to a felony warrant. Officer Lackey located the vehicle, conducted a traffic stop, and confirmed the driver was the wanted individual. The suspect was taken into custody without incident. The warrant was related to a series of bias-motivated stalking cases in downtown Denver. Denver Police expressed their appreciation for the assistance. The vehicle was towed with a hold at DPDs request.

On March 12th, 2025, officers responded to a Flock license plate reader hit on a stolen vehicle at the Northglenn Marketplace. The vehicle, reported stolen out of Denver, was located parked in the shopping center. Officers conducted surveillance and observed the male driver entering Famous Footwear. Officers contacted and detained the suspect inside the store. During a search of the vehicle, officers discovered suspected fentanyl and methamphetamine. The suspect was charged with unlawful possession of a controlled substance, 1st degree motor vehicle theft and driving with a revoked license.

On January 24th, 2024, Northglenn police used Flock automatic license plate reading cameras to help locate and capture a juvenile suspect in a carjacking that involved a 4-month-old baby. After the vehicle was stolen with the infant inside, officers relied on Flock technology to track the car. A Flock camera in neighboring Thornton detected the stolen vehicle, leading Thornton police to stop it in unincorporated Adams County. The suspect was arrested without incident, and the baby, who had been safely left by the suspect and found by Good Samaritans, was unharmed and reunited with their parents.

puyallup-wa-pd: On October 23, 2025, the Puyallup Police Department received a Flock Safety alert for a stolen vehicle. On this day, the department was testing a Drone as a First Responder (DFR) program. An autonomous "Air1" drone self dispatched to the alerting location and located the vehicle traveling westbound. A PPD officer briefly positioned behind the vehicle and deployed Starchase, a GPS tracking technology designed to reduce risks to officers and the public during vehicle eluding incidents. Once the suspect began driving recklessly to elude police intervention, officers did not pursue. Instead, the vehicle continued to be monitored using Starchase and Air1. The suspect later collided with another vehicle and fled on foot into a nearby business plaza, where he was located and taken into custody. This incident highlights how ALPR, DFR, and GPS tracking technologies can support more effective and safer responses by maintaining situational awareness while reducing the need for vehicle pursuits.

SPD25-7269: Glendale Av/S 21 st St, Traffic Accident  Pedestrian Fatality

On October 8, 2025, Sparks Police responded to the area of Glendale and South 21 st Street on a report
of a vehicle versus pedestrian accident. Upon arrival, the victim was declared deceased on scene.
Officers located debris they were able to identify as belonging to a Hummer H3. Using FLOCK ALPR
systems, officers located a Hummer traveling eastbound on Glendale at Galletti approximately four
minutes prior to the call for service. Officers were able to trace the path of the Hummer using FLOCK
and traffic cameras. Officers were able to determine a location in the 1500 block of Sky Valley Drive in
Reno where the vehicle had been scanned on multiple occasions using Vigilant Commercial ALPR
system. An unmarked vehicle was able to locate the Hummer, initially it did not appear to have damage
but upon closer inspection, the vehicle appeared to have been hastily repaired. While surveilling the
vehicle, officers located a male identified as the driver who also was determined to have a felony
warrant and was taken in custody without incident.


SPD25-5122: 1410 E Prater Wy #B, Grand Larceny - Firearm

On July 20, 2025, Sparks responded to a local firearm retailer on a report of a stolen firearm.
Employees reported a male entering the store asking to look at a firearm on display just inside the
entrance to the store. The suspect looked at the firearm briefly before concealing it in his waistband
and exiting the store. Surveillance video showed the male enter a black Volvo SUV before traveling
westbound onto East Prater Way. Using the Flock ALPR systems, officers searched for Volvo vehicles
scanned in the nearby area around the time of the theft. Officers were able to determine the vehicle
had been scanned in the area on six occasions the day before the theft and on two occasions the day
of the theft. Using traffic cameras, the vehicle was located a short distance from the business the day
of the theft and turned into the parking lot of the business just before the theft. Officers calculated the
drive time from where the vehicle was last seen on video to when it arrived at the business confirming
it was the same vehicle. The suspect seen taking the firearm was determined to be associated with the
registered owner and probable cause currently exists for his arrest.

SPD24-7425/SP24-7460: S McCarran Bl/E Nugget Av, Vehicle Burglary - $87,716.60 loss of Apple Products

On September 13, 2024, a semi-trailer leaving Sparks arrived in Reno and discovered over $87,000
worth of Apple products had been stolen from the trailer. A review of cameras on the trailer appeared
to show the products being stolen while the semi-trailer was in transit. The video showed what
appeared to be three vehicles working in tandem to stall the semi-trailer, a white Nissan van, a Cadillac
sedan and a gold four door sedan. The suspects appeared to have boarded the trailer while the semi-
trailer was stalled on two separate occasions in the vicinities of McCarran Boulevard and Greg Street
and Glendale Avenue. Officers were able to use the Flock ALPR system to identify the Nissan Sedan
and its distinct marking as well as a black Cadillac sedan. Officers were able to identify the registered
owners and obtain a warrant for an associated apartment in California. Officers located the stolen
property and linked the Sparks cases to a broader retail theft ring from with additional cases in
California and Illinois.

NHP250901040: Pyramid Wy/Disc Dr, Accident Extrication

On September 11, 2025, officers responded to the intersection of Pyramid Way and Disc drive on a
report of an accident involving extrication. Upon arriving on scene, officers determined the suspect
vehicle, described as a baby blue truck, had fled the scene. Officers interviewed witnesses on scene
and were able to develop a partial plate for the vehicle. Patrol contacted the Real Time Information
Center (RTIC) and the Sparks Sergeant assigned to RTIC was able to use traffic cameras along with
Flock ALPR systems was able to locate the vehicle and correct plate which returned to a Chevy
truck. The information was provided to officers from the responsible agency who responded to the
registered owners address, located the vehicle and driver who was arrested for DUI causing death.

Use of Automatic License Plate Recognition Technology

425.1 PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This policy establishes guidelines for the use, maintenance, training, data retention, and associated use of fixed and mobile automatic license plate readers operated by the Town of Duck Police Department in compliance with North Carolina General Statutes � 20-183.30, � 20-183.31, � 20-183.32, and � 20-183.33.

425.1.1 DEFINITIONS
Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) System ( N.C.G.S. 20-183.30(1))  A system of one or more mobile or fixed automated high speed cameras used in combination with computer algorithms to convert images of license plates into computer readable data.

ALPR Alert  A visual and auditory notice that is triggered when the ALPR determines that captured license plate data matches hot list data present in a database.

ALPR Generated License Plate Data  Information, including location, date and time of a license plate reading, the optical character recognition interpreted data, and any
ALPR generated digital photographic image(s) of a vehicles license plate and vehicle it is attached to, generated entirely by the ALPR.

ALPR Operator  A sworn Town of Duck Police Officer, or a vetted staff member, properly trained in the use of ALPR technology, North Carolina State Law, and Departmental policy governing the use of ALPR generated license plate data.

ALPR Search Reason - The justification entered when performing a search of ALPR generated license plate data, to ensure the search is for a valid law enforcement purpose.

Active Hit Protocol - The verification process performed by an ALPR operator who has received an ALPR alert, to independently verify the validly of the ALPR alert.

Ancillary ALPR Data  Data collected by an ALPR that does not contain optical character recognition interpreted data, ALPR generated digital photographic image(s) of a vehicles license plate or any identifiable vehicle. Ancillary ALPR Data is primarily vehicle traffic volumes calculated by the number of detections an ALPR system performs within a given time frame.
Ancillary ALPR data holds no criminal justice or investigatory value and is not considered ALPR generated plate data for dissemination purposes.

Axon Fleet Dashboard - Software that allows users to start and stop camera recording, play recorded videos, and add metadata to videos. The Dashboard also supports the Axon Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) system notifications and responses. Criminal Justice Officer (N.C.G.S. 20-183.30(1d))  A criminal justice officer as defined in G.S. 17C-2 and justice officer as defined in G.S. 17E-2.

Use of Automatic License Plate Recognition Technology - 2

Flock Safety Web Based Software - Program that provides ALPR alerting and search functions, as well as, integration with Axon Fleet ALPR and Axon evidence.com products. Flock Safety Microsoft Camera Management App - Application that provides ALPR alerting and search functions, as well as, integration with Axon Fleet ALPR and Axon evidence.com products.

Flock Safety App for iOS - Application that provides ALPR alerting and limited search functions.

Hot List  License plate numbers of stolen cars, vehicles owned by persons of interest in a criminal investigation, and vehicles associated with national criminal justice databases that are regularly updated. Hot list information can come from a variety of sources, including stolen and wanted vehicle information from the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), as well as AMBER, SILVER and BLUE Alerts. Hot lists serve an officer safety function as well as an investigatory purpose. ALPR operators may manually add license plate numbers to internal hot lists in order to be alerted if and when a vehicle license plate of interest is detected by an ALPR system.

Law Enforcement Purpose (N.C.G.S. 20-183.30(5))  Any of the following:
(a) Actions related to criminal investigations, arrests, prosecutions, post-conviction confinement, or supervision.
(b) Apprehending an individual with an outstanding felony warrant.
(c) Locating a missing or endangered person.
(d) Locating a lost or stolen vehicle.

Law Enforcement Agency (N.C.G.S. 20-183.30(2)) Any agency or officer of the State of North Carolina or any political subdivision thereof who is empowered by the laws of this State to conduct investigations or to make arrests and any attorney, including the Attorney General of North Carolina, authorized by the laws of this State to prosecute or participate in the prosecution of those persons arrested or persons who may be subject to civil actions related to or concerning an arrest.

Missing or Endangered Person (N.C.G.S. 20-183.30(8))  A person who has been identified as a missing or endangered person by at least one of the following:
(a) The National Criminal Information Center.
(b) The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.
(c) A "be on the lookout" bulletin issued by a law enforcement agency.

425.2 POLICY
The availability and use of automatic license plate readers provide opportunities for the enhancement of public safety, criminal investigations and officer safety. It is the policy of the Town of Duck Police Department that all officers abide by this policy and all applicable State Laws when using automatic license plate recognition technology and/or accessing ALPR generated plate data produced by automatic license plate reader systems.

Use of Automatic License Plate Recognition Technology - 3

425.4 OPERATIONS
Use of ALPR technology is restricted to official law enforcement business and may be used in conjunction with any routine patrol operation or criminal investigation. Reasonable suspicion or probable cause is not required before using ALPR technology. No member of this department shall operate ALPR equipment or access ALPR generated license plate data without first completing department-approved training. No ALPR operator may access confidential department, state or federal data unless authorized to do so.

An officer should follow the active hit protocol to verify an ALPR response through the Division of Criminal Investigation Network (DCIN) before taking enforcement action that is based solely on an ALPR alert (N.C.G.S. � 20-183.31).

425.4.1 ACTIVE HIT PROTOCOL
Active hit protocol consists of the following steps:
(a) Compare the ALPR alert to the translation to check for a misread, and
(b) Compare the state listed in the ALPR alert to the state listed on the hot list to verify it matches, and
(c) Run the license plate that generated the ALPR alert through the Division of Criminal Investigation Network (DCIN) to confirm the validity of the ALPR alert.

425.4 USE OF AUTOMATIC LICENSE PLATE READER DATA AND EQUIPMENT
An officer shall follow the active hit protocol to verify an ALPR response through the Division of Criminal Investigation Network (DCIN) before taking enforcement action that is based solely on an ALPR alert.

Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 20-183.31(b), data obtained by the Duck Police Department shall be obtained, accessed, preserved, or disclosed only for law enforcement or criminal justice purposes. Data shall not be used for the enforcement of traffic violations. Any member who violates the provisions of N.C.G.S. 20-183.30, 20-183.31, or 20-183.32 by illegally obtaining, accessing, preserving, or disclosing data obtained in accordance with the aforementioned statutes, may be found guilty of a Class 1 misdemeanor (N.C.G.S. 20-183.33).

Further, misuse of ALPR equipment, software, or associated databases may also subject the user to disciplinary action.
All ALPR generated plate data is the property of the Town of Duck Police Department.

425.5 ADMINISTRATION
The Chief of Police will designate a command staff member to serve as ALPR Manager.

425.5.1 ALPR MANAGER RESPONSIBILITIES
The ALPR Manager is responsible for:

Use of Automatic License Plate Recognition Technology - 4
(a) The management of the Department's ALPR Program including administration and all aspects of the ALPR system(s) operation including, troubleshooting, repair and
maintenance.
(b) Overseeing all ALPR operator training.
(c) Issuing login credentials to ALPR operators.
(d) Conducting an annual audit of the Department's ALPR system use and its effectiveness.
(e) Recommending policy changes to the Chief of Police.

425.6 REQUIRED TRAINING - N.C.G.S. 20-183.31(A)(4)
No member of this department shall operate ALPR equipment or access ALPR generated license plate data without successfully completing the following training:
(a) Flock Safety Alerts Tool Certification Course.
(b) Flock Safety Search Tool Certification Course.
(c) Axon Academy ALPR Training Course.

Flock Safety Administrators must complete the Flock Safety Administrator Certification Training Course within 30 days of being designated as an administrator.

425.7 ALPR GENERATED LICENSE PLATE DATA SEARCHES
Searches of ALPR generated license plate data are limited to a valid law enforcement purpose, or authorized training.

425.7.1 ALPR SEARCH REASON
Each search of ALPR generated license plate data must include an ALPR search reason. The search reason will be the incident number associated with the search, or if unavailable, a brief statement justifying the legality of the search.

425.8 ALPR OPERATOR RESPONSIBILITIES
On-duty ALPR Operators will:
(a) Monitor Axon Fleet ALPR alerts by remaining logged into Axon Fleet Dashboard software on their mobile data terminal.
(b) Monitor Flock Safety ALPR alerts by logging into Flock Safety Web Based Software, Flock Safety Microsoft Camera Management App, Flock Safety App for iOS, or by
enabling ALPR alerts by text on your work or personal cellphone.
(c) Upon receiving an ALPR alert, the ALPR operator will follow Active Hit Protocol to validate alerts.
(d) Once an ALPR alert has been validated, the ALPR operator may take appropriate action based on the type of alert in accordance with state law, policy, and training.
(e) Report any damage to ALPR systems to their immediate supervisor.

Use of Automatic License Plate Recognition Technology - 5

425.9 SUPERVISORY OVERSIGHT - N.C.G.S. 20-183.31(5)
Supervisors will:
(a) Ensure officers are monitoring Axon Fleet ALPR alerts by remaining logged into Axon Fleet Dashboard software on their mobile data terminal.
(b) Ensure officers are monitoring Flock Safety ALPR alerts through Flock Safety Web Based Software, Flock Safety Microsoft Camera Management App, Flock Safety App
for iOS, or by enabling ALPR alerts by text on their work or personal cellphone.
(c) Monitor ALPR usage by officers to ensure they are in compliance with this policy and North Carolina State Law.
(d) Report any damage to ALPR systems to the ALPR Manager.

425.10 DATABASES/HOTLISTS USED
The Duck Police Department shall maintain and memorandum of understanding with the N.C. State Bureau of Investigation (NCSBI) to memorialize the understanding between our two agencies regarding the transmission of information from the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) Vehicle File, License Plate File, and vehicle information from the NCIC Wanted Person File. Flock Safety and Axon will receive the (NCIC) Vehicle File, License Plate File, and vehicle information from the NCIC Wanted Person File (databases) from the NCSBI, on behalf of the Duck Police Department and will upload the data to fixed and mobile ALPR systems, at least once every
24-hours in accordance with N.C.G.S. 20-183.32(d).

In addition, the Town of Duck Police Department will maintain an agency wide hot list of license plates significant to criminal investigations being conducted internally or in cooperation with another law enforcement agency. Individual ALPR operators may create and maintain their own hot list of license plates significant to criminal investigations being conducted internally or in cooperation with another law enforcement agency.

425.11 DATA STORAGE AND RETENTION (N.C.G.S.20-183.32)
Captured plate data that has been captured by an ALPR system owned or leased by the Town of Duck Police Department shall not be preserved for more than 90 days after the date the data is captured, unless the captured plate data is subject to preservation for more than 90 days pursuant to any of the following:
1. A search warrant issued pursuant to Article 11 of Chapter 15A of the North Carolina General Statutes.
2. A federal search warrant issued in compliance with the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure.
3. Upon the request of a law enforcement agency's written, sworn statement, that includes all of the following:

Use of Automatic License Plate Recognition Technology - 6
(a) The location of the particular camera or cameras for which captured plate data must be preserved and the particular license plate for which captured plate data must be preserved.
(b) The date or dates and time frames for which captured plate data must be preserved.
(c) Specific and articulable facts showing that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the captured plate data is relevant and material to an ongoing criminal or missing persons investigation or is needed to prove a violation of a motor carrier safety regulation.
(d) The case and identity of the parties involved in that case.

425.11.1 ANCILLARY ALPR DATA

Ancillary ALPR data is not governed by North Carolina State Law and is not subject to any retention or use regulations.

425.12 CRIMINAL JUSTICE INTERAGENCY ALPR GENERATED LICENSE PLATE DATA AND HOT LIST SHARING

ALPR generated license plate data shall not be disclosed except to a criminal justice officer at a state or local law enforcement agency or a similar official at a federal law enforcement agency for a legitimate law enforcement purpose pursuant to a written request from the requesting agency. Requests may be in electronic format.

The Duck Police Department will limit the sharing of its ALPR generated license plate data and its internal hot list to the following:
(a) Federal law enforcement agencies nationwide.
(b) State and local law enforcement agencies in North Carolina.

425.13 INTERNAL DATA SECURITY - N.C.G.S. 20-183.31(6)

ALPR operators must have a valid username and password to access ALPR generated plate data through Flock and Axon software.

425.14 ALPR EQUIPMENT MAINTENANCE AND MODIFICATION - N.C.G.S. 20-183.31(C)

All ALPR system maintenance, and calibrations (if applicable), performed by members or contractors shall be logged and maintained on file indefinitely. ALPR equipment shall not be modified without authorization from the Chief of Police.

425.15 PUBLIC DISCLOSURE OF RECORDS

Captured plate data obtained in accordance with North Carolina Law is confidential and not a
public record as that term is defined in N.C.G.S. 132-1. Captured plate data shall not be sold for any purpose.

Use of Automatic License Plate Recognition Technology - 7

425.16 ANNUAL AUDITING AND REPORTING OF ALPR USE AND EFFECTIVENESS
The ALPR Manager shall conduct an annual audit and presenting a report of the Department's ALPR system use and its effectiveness to the Chief of Police on or before November 1st of each year.

425.17 ALPR GENERATED LICENSE PLATE DATA CAPTURED OUTSIDE OF AN OFFICER'S JURISDICTION

Pursuant to 421.4, the Axon Fleet in-car camera system shall remain on at all times when the patrol vehicle is in use. When an Axon Fleet in-car camera is on, it will detect and process license plate data. This will lead to the capture of license plate data outside of the Town of Duck during an officers commute and when an officer is out of his or her jurisdiction for approved travel. If an ALPR operator receives an ALPR alert while outside of his or her jurisdiction, if safe to do so, the ALPR operator should follow the active hit protocol. If the hit is confirmed, the ALPR operator should notify on-duty officers in the jurisdiction where the suspect vehicle was last seen. The officer
will not take enforcement action unless requested to do so pursuant to a mutual aid request.

arvada-co-pd:
The summaries below provide real examples of how ALPR data has contributed to arrests, vehicle recoveries and investigative breakthroughs, including violent crime cases. These examples also demonstrate how the system is used responsibly, including instances where alerts helped exonerate someone and prevent unnecessary enforcement action.


Cases are listed in chronological order, beginning with the most recent.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR26002067 | Jan. 28, 2026 | Suspicious Incident

Police received a report that an individual was seen dragging what appeared to be a person into a minivan. Officers responded but were unable to locate the vehicle. During an area canvass, investigators obtained surveillance video showing a white male exiting a gray minivan on West 57th Avenue. The male placed a backpack on a bench inside Wolff Park, returned to the vehicle, then appeared to drag an unconscious or possibly deceased person to the rear and opposite side of the minivan before placing the individual back inside and driving westbound.

Based on the video, the situation appeared extremely concerning and potentially involved a homicide. Investigators searched Flock ALPR cameras in the area and located the minivan. Using the captured license plate, officers contacted the registered owner and determined the driver had picked up a family member experiencing substance abuse issues and initially wanted to drop him in the park to sleep. The driver then became concerned and transported the family member to a hospital for medical attention, which investigators confirmed with hospital staff.

Impact: ALPR technology allowed investigators to quickly identify the vehicle and determine that no crime had occurred. Without ALPR data, the incident could have remained an active and resource-intensive investigation involving a suspected body disposal.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR2600018 | Jan. 1, 2026 | Auto Theft


A Flock alert identified a stolen vehicle at Home Depot. The vehicle was later located near Harkins Theatre, and the suspect was taken into custody.


Impact: ALPR provided real-time location information that led to rapid recovery of the vehicle and the arrest of the suspect.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25022781 | Dec. 26, 2025 | Recovered Stolen Vehicle


A Flock alert notified officers that a stolen vehicle was in the area. When officers attempted contact, the suspects fled and crashed before fleeing on foot. Evidence was recovered from the scene, and the investigation continued.


Impact: ALPR allowed officers to quickly locate a stolen vehicle, resulting in recovery and additional investigative evidence.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25022515 | Dec. 21, 2025 | Felony Menacing


An ALPR camera alerted officers to a vehicle connected to a hit-and-run investigation. Officers attempted contact with the suspect, who produced an edged weapon and barricaded himself inside the van. After negotiations, the suspect surrendered and was jailed on felony menacing and related charges.


Impact: ALPR helped officers locate a suspect and resolve a dangerous situation safely.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25017866 | Oct. 11, 2025 | Carjacking / Attempted Homicide


After a shooting, suspects stole the victims vehicle. The Jefferson County Sheriffs Office monitored Flock alerts and was notified when the vehicle passed a camera. Deputies located and pursued the vehicle, ultimately arresting both suspects.


Impact: Regional ALPR collaboration enabled rapid cross-jurisdictional identification and arrest in a violent felony case.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25017405 | Oct. 4, 2025 | Attempted Murder


Detectives investigated a shooting involving two vehicles. Through interviews, one vehicle was determined to be uninvolved. The suspect vehicle was identified using ALPR data. Investigators noted that the ALPR identification was the first critical lead in the case. Without it, the investigation likely would have stalled. The identification ultimately led to the arrest of the shooter.


Impact: ALPR served as the key investigative breakthrough that led to a successful arrest in a shooting case.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25008595 | May 22, 2025 | Vehicular Assault


A teenage couple became involved in an argument. During the incident, the female jumped onto the hood of a white Chevrolet, fell off and was run over, sustaining serious injuries including a broken pelvis. The driver fled. Officers used Flock cameras in the area to identify the vehicle and obtain a license plate number. That information allowed investigators to locate and later charge the driver.


Impact: ALPR data quickly identified a fleeing vehicle in a serious injury case, resulting in the arrest of a suspect.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25007636 | May 8, 2025 | Fatal Hit-and-Run


A person using a personal mobility chair was struck and killed by a pickup truck whose driver fled the scene. Investigators searched nearby Flock cameras and quickly identified a possible suspect vehicle and license plate. Additional ALPR data helped investigators determine it was not with the registered owner, leading to identification and arrest of the suspect.


Impact: ALPR provided critical early leads in a fatal crash investigation, accelerating suspect identification.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25022885 | April 28, 2025 | Auto Theft (Exclusionary Use)


A Flock alert indicated a stolen vehicle at Home Depot. Officers contacted the driver inside the store. The investigation revealed the driver had permission to possess the vehicle and that the stolen entry from another jurisdiction was incorrect. The alert allowed officers to safely resolve the issue without incident.


Impact: ALPR enabled officers to clear a records error and prevent unnecessary escalation.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25007074 | April 28, 2025 | Auto Theft (Exclusionary Use)


A Flock alert identified a stolen work van traveling on Ralston Road. Before initiating a stop, officers contacted the registered owner, who confirmed he was driving the vehicle and had mistakenly reported it stolen.


Impact: ALPR allowed officers to verify information before taking enforcement action, preventing an unnecessary stop.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25006276 | April 15, 2025 | Auto Theft / Felony Menacing


An officer received a Flock alert while patrolling for a stolen vehicle. The vehicle was found occupied at an apartment complex. The female driver was arrested for First-Degree Motor Vehicle Theft. A second stolen vehicle parked next to it was also recovered. Evidence related to a felony menacing case involving a firearm from the previous night was recovered from one of the vehicles.


Impact: One ALPR alert led to two stolen vehicle recoveries, an arrest and evidence recovery tied to a violent crime.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25004818 | March 22, 2025 | Felony Warrants


An ALPR alert identified a stolen license plate. Officers located the vehicle and contacted the occupants. Both were arrested on outstanding felony warrants.


Impact: ALPR facilitated the safe apprehension of wanted individuals.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25002192 | Feb. 7, 2025 | Auto Theft


An ALPR alert identified a stolen vehicle. The suspect was located and charged with motor vehicle theft and drug possession.


Impact: ALPR supported vehicle recovery and the arrest of the suspect.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR25000692 | Jan. 13, 2025 | Armed Carjacking (Juvenile Suspects)


Juveniles pistol-whipped a driver at a Lakewood gas station and stole his Jeep at gunpoint. Shortly after, a Flock camera later detected the stolen Jeep in Arvada. Officers located the vehicle, and after a brief pursuit, safely stopped it. Three juvenile suspects were taken into custody. A .40-caliber Glock handgun equipped with an illegal auto switch was recovered. Two suspects were linked to additional auto theft investigations.


Impact: ALPR detection enabled rapid identification and safe apprehension of armed carjacking suspects.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR24018646 | Nov. 1, 2024 | Auto Theft


An ALPR alert identified a stolen vehicle. Contact with the occupants resulted in one arrest for motor vehicle theft and another arrest on outstanding warrants.


Impact: ALPR contributed to stolen vehicle recovery and the arrest of wanted individuals.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR24015422 | Sept. 8, 2024 | Vehicular Assault


Following a vehicle sale dispute, a suspect intentionally struck a motorcyclist. Investigators searched ALPR cameras for a matching vehicle description. The search identified the suspect vehicle, including matching damage. Later that day, another agency recovered the vehicle, and the driver was arrested.


Impact: ALPR provided rapid suspect vehicle identification in an intentional assault case.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

AR23012579 | Aug. 8, 2023 | At-Risk Adult / Cybercrime Investigation


An ALPR alert identified a vehicle connected to an active investigation involving theft from an at-risk adult, identity theft and a theft series. Officers contacted the suspects based on the alert, and charges were filed.


Impact: ALPR helped investigators locate suspects involved in financial exploitation of a vulnerable community member.
bridgewater-va-pd:
- BPD had a rash of catalytic converters stolen in town as well around the surrounding areas. Through the work of our police department and the Flock service, we were able to identify the vehicle and track down the suspect through the cameras, ultimately leading to an arrest, multiple charges in 6 jurisdictions, and seizing $26,000 in cash from the offender from stolen catalytic sales.

- Another recent crime involved a check fraud at a local bank; using the Flock service we were able to identify the vehicle from the little information that was provided from the teller and identify the vehicle owner and suspect within 20 minutes of the incident.

-August 2023 Success Story: An expensive motorcycle helmet was stolen from outside of the 7-11 convenience store in Bridgewater. The stores cameras were only able to capture part of the truck, giving us the color and body style. Using our Flock camera system, we were able to observe a truck matching the color and body style leaving the town on Dinkel Avenue. Using the license plate from the Flock footage, we were able to identify the vehicles owner. Officers went to the suspects home retrieved the helmet. This case was solved, and the property was returned to its rightful owner.
cedar-lake-in-pd:
On August 2, 2025, Cedar Lake Police were assisting in the investigation of a fatal hit-and-run accident. Investigating officers used nearby surveillance video and evidence left at the scene; the fleeing vehicle was identified only as a gold-colored pick-up truck. Using Flock Safety, a search was performed of nearby cameras, and a vehicle was positively identified. Officers were able to locate the vehicle, a gold Ford Ranger, that had damage consistent with the accident, and the driver was identified and taken into custody.

On December 26, 2023, Officers were dispatched to a hit-and-run crash with injuries. The victim, a resident of Cedar Lake, was struck by a gold SUV, which fled the scene. The victim sustained injuries, and their vehicle sustained severe damage. The resident was able to take a photo of the offending vehicle. A license plate was not recognizable; however, there was a distinctive marking on the rear of the vehicle. Damaged parts left at the scene were traced to a Ford Escape. Using Flock Safety, a search was performed for a Ford SUV near the time of the accident. A vehicle was positively identified with the same distinctive marking provided by the victim. Investigators followed up with the Offender, who resides in a nearby community, located the fleeing vehicle, and positively identified the suspect.

On February 7, 2024, Officers were dispatched to a hit-and-run crash. The victim described the vehicle as a silver truck with a "for sale" sign. Using nearby security cameras, Officers determined that the offending vehicle was a Silver Toyota Tundra. Using Flock Safety, a search was performed for a Silver Toyota Tundra near the time of the accident. A vehicle was positively identified. Officers followed up, locating the vehicle, and positively identified the suspect.
charlottesville-va-pd:
1. A stolen vehicle from our jurisdiction was alerted on our cameras several times after being stolen. It then went to a neighboring jurisdiction with Flock cameras and was alerted on theirs. The officer responded and found the vehicle occupied. The vehicle attempted to flee and rammed the patrol car and was taken into custody on scene.

2. Out of jurisdiction, stolen vehicle alerted on our cameras. Officers were able to pinpoint where the vehicle was alerting, recover the vehicle unoccupied, and recover evidence from inside the vehicle.

3. Out of jurisdiction stolen vehicle was alerted on our N Emmet St. Officers in the area located the vehicle, and a pursuit was initiated. The vehicle was later recovered unoccupied, and evidence was recovered.

4. Out of jurisdiction individual wanted for homicide alerted on our N Emmet St camera. Based on this alert, we notified that jurisdiction that the vehicle was likely headed back in their direction. Their officers were able to stop the vehicle as it crossed their county line. The subject was taken into custody shortly after.

5. The suspect vehicle involved in a shooting within our jurisdiction was identified on the Flock system. Based on this information, the driver was identified and ultimately charged with the incident when confronted with the Flock results.
dayton-oh-pd:
On February 26, 2026, officers were alerted by a Flock camera that a stolen motorcycle was traveling westbound on Boltin Street passing Nassau Street. Officers began to saturate the area to look for the motorcycle. A lieutenant located the motorcycle, which had turned off its lights, and stopped it in the 1400 block of McLain Street. The suspect was arrested without incident.

On February 19, 2026, officers were alerted by a Flock camera that a felonious assault suspect vehicle was traveling westbound on West Third Street near North Gettysburg Avenue. Officers began checking the area and obtained additional information on the vehicle registration. Officers then located the vehicle in the 400 block of Crown Avenue and made a traffic stop. Their investigation led to an arrest and the recovery of a firearm.

On January 12, 2026, officers were investigating a missing adult complaint involving a 97-year-old female with dementia who apparently had driven off in her vehicle without taking her phone or purse. Officers were able to utilize Flock cameras to start checking areas the vehicle had been captured on the cameras. In less than an hour, officers located the vehicle and female who was safe and unharmed. She was then reunited her with her family.

On January 7, 2026, officers received a stolen vehicle alert from a Flock camera at North Gettysburg and Kammer Avenue. While driving through the area they located the vehicle unoccupied in the 4000 block of Kammer Avenue. The vehicle was stolen out of Riverside, Ohio. While recovering the stolen vehicle they located a firearm in the vehicle.

On December 23, 2025, officers received a stolen vehicle alert from a Flock camera at Stanley Avenue and Kuntz Road. The vehicle fled from a Metro Parks officer at which time several officers began looking for the vehicle. The vehicle was located and recovered in the 2700 block of Triangle View Drive.

On December 14, 2025, officers were investigating an armed robbery complaint at the UDF located at 1943 E. Siebenthaler Avenue. Using Flock cameras, a suspect vehicle was identified which led to identifying a suspect. The suspect and vehicle were located the next day at which time the suspect was arrested.

On November 24, 2025, officers were informed of a Flock Safety camera alert on stolen license plate affixed to the rear of a dark blue Chevy Malibu near Summit Square apartments. Officers located the vehicle a short time later traveling on Hoover Avenue. Officers attempted to make a traffic stop, but the vehicle fled. Ohio State Patrol Aviation was working, and the vehicle was located near the intersection of Sylvan Drive and Circle Road unoccupied. However, both occupants were located and arrested. In addition to recovering the stolen license plate, the vehicle was also reported as stolen.

On November 4, 2025, an officer received a Flock Safety camera alert on a stolen vehicle in the area around Steve Whalen Boulevard at US35. Officers attempted a stop on the vehicle at which time it fled. Ohio State Patrol Aviation was working as part of a violent crime reduction operation and was able to keep a visual on the stolen vehicle. The two occupants fled from the vehicle on Epworth Avenue. Both occupants were taken into custody. In addition to recovering the stolen vehicle, officers also recovered a handgun.

On October 27, 2025, officers were aware of a Flock Safety camera alert on a stolen vehicle. The officers located the vehicle a short time later in the parking lot of 4675 Hoover Avenue. Their investigation resulted in the apprehension of a male subject who had just parked the stolen vehicle.

On October 16, 2025, an officer working in the Real Time Crime Center was alerted by a hit from a Flock Safety camera involving a sexual assault suspect vehicle. A broadcast was made over the radio to officers on patrol. A sergeant made a traffic stop on the vehicle and located the suspect in the vehicle at which time the suspect was taken into custody.

On September 10, 2025, two individuals were allegedly firing handguns at one another from moving vehicles in the area of North Gettysburg Avenue and North James H. McGee Boulevard, which resulted in a hit-and-run accident involving an uninvolved third party. The Real-Time Crime Center was able to utilize Flock cameras, in conjunction with RTCC databases, to provide identifying information on the vehicles and individuals involved to the responding crews.

On September 3, 2025, the McDonalds at 1219 North Gettysburg Avenue was robbed by two suspects. The suspects brandished a firearm and assaulted an employee. Using Flock cameras, the Real-Time Crime Center was able to narrow down the suspect vehicle, identify the license plate, and utilize other information sources to identify both suspects. (The firearm used in this Aggravated Robbery was subsequently located during follow-up investigation and linked to an additional domestic violence-related Felonious Assault.)

On August 14, 2025, officers began checking the area of Summit Square Drive after receiving information from another officer regarding a recent Flock Safety alert for a stolen vehicle in the area. Officers located the vehicle and detained two suspects. Detectives later interviewed both individuals, who were subsequently arrested for receiving stolen property. The recovered vehicle had been reported stolen out of Butler County.

On August 1, 2025, while on patrol, officers received a Flock Safety alert regarding a vehicle connected to an aggravated menacing offense, reportedly in the area of West Siebenthaler and Salem Avenue. Officers located the vehicle as it turned into the Shell gas station parking lot in the 3600 block of North Main Street. As officers entered the lot, two passengers exited the vehicle and attempted to walk away, but were quickly detained. The driver remained inside the vehicle. As a result of the investigation, two individuals were arrested, a large quantity of marijuana and a rifle were recovered, and the vehicle was towed from the scene.

On July 10, 2025, officers located an Aggravated Robbery vehicle with the assistance of Flock cameras. The vehicle was taken earlier in the morning, and a traffic stop was attempted on the vehicle around Parkland Avenue. The vehicle failed to comply, and a pursuit ensued. The pursuit traveled throughout various parts of Dayton. The vehicle then began traveling northbound on I-75. An officer was able to conduct a PIT maneuver on the vehicle, ending the pursuit in Miami County. The adult male driver was taken into custody without further incident.

On June 28, 2025, a sergeant was on patrol around Lathrop Avenue and Hawker Street, checking the area where a stolen vehicle had just been captured on FLOCK cameras. Three juveniles were located walking away from the car, and upon seeing the sergeant, two of the three juveniles fled upon his approach. Multiple crews were quick to respond, and due to the fast response and a great job setting up a perimeter, a Kettering PD K9 was able to conduct a successful track and found the other two juveniles hiding in the bushes of a nuisance-abated property. A general assignment unit callout was initiated. All three juveniles were booked into the Juvenile Justice Center for receiving stolen property and other various charges related to the incident.

On May 24, 2025, officers were dispatched on a shooting complaint in the 2200 block of Rugby Road. Upon arrival, officers located the victim suffering from a non-life-threatening gunshot wound to the upper left chest, and the victim was removed to MVH for further medical treatment. A diligent investigation revealed a potential suspect vehicle. With the assistance of Flock cameras and video footage from a neighbor, the suspect vehicle was identified. Officers from the Real-Time Crime Center were able to update crews on the vehicle's location using technology at their disposal, including Flock cameras.
