column1: Cottage Grove PD Policy
cottage-grove-wi-pd:
I. PURPOSE

A. The purpose of this document is to establish guidelines for all sworn personnel of
the Cottage Grove Police Department to ensure a uniform approach to traffic
law violation enforcement by the department. A great number of contacts
between officers and citizens are traffic-oriented. The goal of this policy is not to
supplant officer judgment in those contacts. The goal is to provide a uniform
traffic enforcement policy that will assist officers in performing this function, as
well as satisfy the public's right to expect uniformity in traffic enforcement.

II. POLICY

A. It is the policy of the Cottage Grove Police Department that officers shall enforce
traffic laws in a fair and equitable manner with the goal of achieving voluntary
compliance with traffic laws and regulations. The responsibility for enforcing
traffic laws is shared by all uniformed personnel. Enforcement action taken by
officers shall be in accordance with applicable traffic laws and ordinances and
shall consider the degree and severity of the violation. Officers shall conduct
themselves in a courteous, business-like manner during all traffic contacts.

B. Supervisors shall develop a selective traffic enforcement program for their
assigned teams. The selective enforcement programs shall utilize various
selective enforcement techniques and be based on an analysis of traffic crashes
and traffic law violation experience. The programs shall be evaluated and
modified as necessary, on an annual basis.

III. DISCUSSION

IV. DEFINITIONS

A. Area Patrol  Patrol or stationary observation in an area that includes many
streets, roads, or sections of highway.

B. Covert Observation  Stationary observation in which the observer is not visible
from the roadway by persons using ordinary powers of observation.

C. Custodial Arrest  Any enforcement action that results in taking persons into
custody for holding or detaining them to answer a violation of the law before a
court.

D. Hazardous Violation  A traffic law violation that poses a direct threat to the safe
movement of vehicular or pedestrian traffic.

E. Line Patrol  Moving patrol or stationary observation of a specified route
between two points, usually on one Village street or a section of a highway.

F. Non-Hazardous Violation  A traffic law violation that does not pose a direct
threat to the safe movement of vehicular or pedestrian traffic.

G. Selective Traffic Enforcement  The assignment of personnel to traffic
enforcement activities at times or locations where hazardous or congested
conditions exist. Such assignments are usually based on such factors as traffic
volume, crash experience, and frequency of traffic violations.

H. Stationary Observation  Traffic observation at a selected place, usually one with
an unfavorable crash experience or a traffic flow problem, for traffic law
enforcement purposes, particularly to detect violations or deter possible
violators.

I. Traffic Law Violation  Violation of any statute, ordinance or any legally
authorized regulation relating to the use of streets and highways or the
operation and ownership of motor vehicles and other road vehicles.

J. Visible Observation  Stationary observation by one observer in full view, but so
located, such as on a side street, that effort is required by those in the traffic
stream to discover the observer.

K. Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) system  a computer-based system
that utilizes cameras to capture license plate information. The ALPR system
passively captures an infrared image of license plates on moving vehicles and
converts them to a text file using Optical Character Recognition. The text is
compared to hot lists generated by law enforcement agencies, including the
National Crime Information Center (NCIC), the Crime Information Bureau (CIB),
the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (WisDOT), and the local agency.
The ALPR system generates an alert when there is a hit. The ALPR system also
transmits and stores the digital images of license plates and vehicles and associated metadata (e.g., date, time, and geographic coordinates associated
with the vehicle image capture) on the server. The stored ALPR data can be
queried by license plate number, time frame, description, and location, and will
return the reads matching the search criteria. Stored ALPR data is not associated
with and will not identify any person who is operating a vehicle.

L. Alarm/Hit -- a positive indication by visual and/or audio signal of a potential
match of data on the "Hot List" and the license plate scanned by the ALPR. (A
"hit" is not conclusive confirmation that a license plate is wanted. Additional
investigation is always warranted when a "hit" is indicated.)

M. Hot List -- a list of license plates of specific concern to the investigative and/or
enforcement interests of law enforcement that is transmitted to an ALPR to a
fixed system, or a portable system.

N. ALPR Administrator -- Employee charged with coordinating all aspects of the
ALPR system for the Cottage Grove Police Department.

O. ALPR Operator -- a Cottage Grove Police Department employee who has been
officially trained in the lawful use of the ALPR(s).

P. ALPR Alert -- a visible and audible notification to an ALPR Operator that a license
plate scanned by an ALPR is on a prepared hot list.

Q. Fixed ALPR System -- ALPR cameras that are permanently affixed to a structure, a
pole, a traffic barrier, or a bridge.

R. Plate Reads -- the associated image and data of a license that is scanned by an
ALPR camera.


V. PROCEDURE

A. Traffic Law Enforcement Activities

a. Officers shall take appropriate enforcement action when they have
probable cause to believe, either through personal observation or after
an investigation, that a state traffic law or Village traffic ordinance
violation has occurred.

b. It is not the intent of this policy to foresee every possible situation that
may arise, nor is an officer's judgment to be supplanted in such matters.
A traffic law violation may be handled by officers with a written warning,
a traffic citation, or a custodial arrest.

c. The course of action taken by the officer shall be determined by the
circumstances of the incident and shall be left to the officer's discretion.
The guidance to officers in this policy is intended to assist officers in
exercising that discretion fairly and effectively.

d. Officers shall exercise discretion in electing the type of enforcement
action to be taken in accordance with the following criteria:

1. The weather, condition of the roadway, volume of other traffic,
and the presence of pedestrians in the area should be considered
by the officer.

2. Whether the violation was intentional or inadvertent.

3. The seriousness of the violation includes whether the violation
may have resulted in injury and/or property damage.

4. The extent of any injury and/or property damage.
5. If the enforcement action protects the interests of other people
or drivers involved in the incident.

6. If the enforcement action accomplishes a legitimate police
purpose.

7. If the violator committed similar violations in the past.

8. If, in the officer's judgment, the proposed enforcement action will
be sufficient to deter the violator from committing similar
violations in the future.
e. Officers should consider the following guidelines when determining the
type of enforcement action to take:

1. Written Warning: The least severe enforcement action would be
appropriate in cases involving very minor and inadvertent traffic
law or equipment violations where the person readily
acknowledges the violation. The officer should be satisfied that
the person will not repeat the violation, and no further
enforcement action is needed.

2. Citation: Traffic citations are appropriate for more serious
infractions, intentional violations, violations resulting in injury, or
property damage, and for most infractions that are determined to
be the cause of a traffic crash. Citations may also be appropriate,
even for minor infractions, when the officer determines the
violator's prior traffic history or his/her demeanor with the officer
indicates that a written warning would have little impact on
deterring future traffic violations of a similar nature.

3. Custodial Arrest: Officer discretion is somewhat limited once the
officer has elected to arrest for OWI or a Section II criminal traffic
offense found in the Traffic Deposit Schedule. Officers shall
follow the procedures in the OWI Policy and/or ARREST Policy of
this department, as applicable, for release procedures after a
custodial arrest has been made.

B. Officers Actions during Traffic Contacts with Motorists

a. Officers shall conduct themselves in a courteous, business-like manner
during traffic contacts.

b. Officers should not argue with motorists on the merits of the
enforcement action taken, nor should they be dissuaded from taking
enforcement action unless extenuating circumstances are clearly present.

c. Officers should explain why the course of enforcement action is being
taken, the elements of the offense, if requested, and the consequences
of the enforcement action, if any.

d. Officers shall provide motorists with the following information if a
citation or custodial arrest is made:

1. Offense information.
2. The court appearance time and date for the traffic offense.
3. For a criminal offense for which no traffic citation is issued, a
mandatory court date for appearance in Circuit Court.
4. Whether a court appearance is mandatory.
5. Information regarding citation payment.

C. Officer Safety during Traffic Stops

a. Officer safety shall be a primary consideration when taking any traffic
enforcement action.

b. Initial Stop of a Motorist

1. Officers should choose the location for a traffic stop carefully to
avoid hills, curves, and intersections that may cause danger from
other traffic to the officer and the person stopped.

2. Officers should be aware of their location and immediate
surroundings, should it be necessary to seek cover during the
stop.

3. The location of the stop, and the vehicle's registration number
and state, or a complete description of the vehicle if the vehicle
has no registration plates, shall be called into the dispatch center
before or immediately after the traffic stop.

4. Authorized emergency lighting shall be used to initiate a stop and
until the stop is completed. The use of 4-way flashers or blinking
yellow lights on the overhead light bar are not authorized in lieu
of the red and blue lights and do not provide the legal protection
of WI SS 347.25. However, they may be used in addition to the
red and blue lights on the police vehicle.

5. Officers should position their police vehicle to the rear and slightly
off center to protect the officer from other traffic while
approaching the stopped vehicle.

c. Initial Contact with a Motorist

1. Utilizing headlamps and take-down lamps at night, officers should
observe the occupants of the vehicle before and during the
approach to the vehicle for unusual activity. Officers should
position themselves behind the driver's door to avoid sudden
opening of the door when making the initial contact with the
driver and should continue observation of all occupants of the
vehicle, including those in the back seat or back of a van or truck.

2. Wanted and driver status checks on the operator and any
passengers for whom the officer has identifying information
should be made. The officer should maintain frequent visual contact with the vehicle and occupants while completing the
warning or citation.

3. Officers hearing radio traffic of a stop by another officer in the
area should drive by that location to ensure the officer's safety or
render assistance, as necessary.

4. Delivery of the warning or citation should be made in the same
manner as the initial approach to the vehicle, using all
precautions. The officer should let the stopped vehicle exit the
area first and should not extinguish emergency lighting until the
officer intends to re-enter the flow of traffic.

D. Non-Approach Contacts

a. There may be times when your threat assessment leads you to conclude
that the situation is a non-approach contact but does not rise to the level
of a high-risk contact. Examples of this may be vehicles with multiple
occupants or vehicles stopped in a Terry type context. In these
situations, the officer may wait for back-up to arrive prior to any contact
with the occupants of the vehicle.

b. When confronted with a non-approach contact, the officer may position
their vehicle differently than in an approach contact. The officer may
choose to use an angle left position to use the engine block of their squad
for cover. If the officer chooses to use the offset position, the officer
should consider creating a greater distance between their squad and the
subject vehicle, as distance provides the officer with more of an
opportunity to react to actions of the occupants of the subject vehicle.

c. Generally, in a non-approach contact, the officer will direct the occupants
of the vehicle out of the vehicle. The officer may choose to exit their
squad prior to giving directions to the occupants of the vehicle. This
allows the officer to see the occupants of the vehicle better. When an
officer chooses to exit their squad, they should utilize any cover or
concealment available.

E. High-Risk Contacts

a. In a high-risk contact, the officer will not approach the vehicle until all the
occupants have been ordered out of the vehicle at gunpoint and the
vehicle has been secured. High-risk contacts require at least two,preferably more officers, to conduct.

The following are factors an officer
should consider in determining whether to conduct a high-risk contact:

1. The nature of the offense.
2. Occupants with warrants for violent offenses.
3. Pursuits.
4. An occupant with a violent history.

b. Officers conducting a high-risk vehicle contact should use the following
procedure:

1. Contact Dispatch and Coordinate Responding Squads

" An officer who decides to perform a high-risk stop should
provide dispatch with as much information about the
vehicle as possible. The officer should notify dispatch of
the plate number of the vehicle, make, color, and number
of occupants in the vehicle. The officer shall notify
dispatch of the reason for the contact, the intent to make
a high-risk stop, and the need for additional units to
perform the stop. The officer should continue to follow
the vehicle, update other squads as to the location of the
vehicle (speed and location), and any behavior of the
occupants of the vehicle.

" As other squads respond to your location, communicate
with them as to where you intend to perform the stop,
and if possible, coordinate the roles of the officers.

" Due to the nature of high-risk stops and the need for
coordination, officers are assigned specific roles to play
during the stop. These roles include:

(i) Contact Officer: The contact officer communicates
with the occupants of the subject vehicle, using the
squad PA system or other means.

(ii) Cover Officer(s): Each cover officer is assigned an
area of responsibility that contains one or more
problem areas.

(iii) Arrest Control Officer(s): Each arrest control officer
takes care of handcuffing, searching, and gathering
intelligence from suspects removed from the
subject vehicle and brought back to the squads.

(iv) Traffic Control Officer(s): Traffic control officers
maintain the perimeters of the scene to control
traffic and prevent interference with the scene.

(v) Forward Observer: If the environment is such that
cover or concealment is available, a forward
observer can provide information about the subject
vehicle and its occupants. A forward observer
must be careful not to take up a position that
would create a crossfire situation.

" Not all high-risk stops will have enough officers to fulfill
these roles. However, it is recommended that at a
minimum, three officers are utilized to perform the
contact, cover, and arrest control roles.

2. Performing the Stop

" In performing a high-risk stop, squads should be
positioned at least fifty feet away from the subject vehicle.
Two squads should be positioned behind the subject
vehicle at a slight angle to one another. These squads
should use all their lights (emergency lights, take-down
lights, spotlights) to illuminate the suspect vehicle
regardless of the time of day. Only the two front-line
squads should have their headlights, take-down lights,
spotlights, and forward-facing emergency lights activated.
This is done to avoid back-lighting the officers in front.

" Once the vehicle is stopped and other squads are in
position, officers should take up tactical positions behind
their squads. Contact and cover officers should position
themselves behind the pillars of the squad. These officers
should draw their service weapons and train them on the
suspect vehicle in a tactical ready position. Officers should
consider using available long guns if practical. Officers
acting as arrest control officers shall have their weapons drawn until they approach to handcuff the occupants of
the vehicle. Any other officers to the rear of the front-line
squads should not have their weapons drawn.

3. Order Occupants out of Vehicle

" Only one officer, the contact officer, should provide the
commands. If available, the contact officer should give the
commands through the squad's PA system. The officer
should use clear, concise, and unemotional dialogue in
providing commands.

" The officer shall identify which subject in the vehicle he is
providing commands to. The officer will start by ordering
the driver out of the vehicle. The driver should be ordered
to direct the occupants to open the windows and turn the
car off. Direct the driver to turn on the dome light and
turn off the radio. Order the occupants to release their
seatbelts and immediately return their hands to where the
officer can see them. Direct the operator to remove the
keys from the ignition, place both hands out of the
window, and place the keys on the roof of the vehicle.

" Order the driver to exit the vehicle through the drivers
door. The driver should be told to open the door with his
hands outside of the window, using the outside handle to
open the door, and their feet to push the door open. The
officer should order the driver to face away from the
squads and step away from the vehicle, order the driver to
slowly turn 360 degrees, and order the driver to walk
slowly backwards towards the sound of your voice.

" If an officer observes a weapon while the subject is turning
around, the officer shall inform other officers of his/her
observations. The subject should be ordered to continue
to walk backwards to the sound of the officers voice. The
officer should clearly warn the subject not to let his/her
hands go near the weapon. Also, the subject should be
warned that any movement may be met with the
appropriate use of force.

" Order the driver to continue to walk backwards to the
selected area for handcuffing. Once in this area, the preferred method is to have the subject kneel for the
handcuffing procedure. Once the subject is kneeling,
order the subject to place their arms out like an airplane,
place their thumbs down, bend forward, bring their arms
backward, and cross their ankles.

" The arrest control officer or contact officer will handcuff
the suspect. The arrest control officer will search the
subject and gather intelligence from the subject. The
arrest control officer will ask the subject about weapons in
the vehicle and the number of occupants.

" The contact officer will direct the other subjects out of the
vehicle, starting with the front seat passenger. The
contact officer will use the same commands as with the
driver, and if possible, have the subjects exit through the
drivers door. The arrest control officer will place
additional subjects in handcuffs as described above. The
arrest control officer will keep the detained subjects
separated if possible.

" Once all the visible occupants have been removed from
the vehicle, the contact officer should verbally challenge
any hidden subjects in the vehicle. The contact officer
should command, not ask, subjects to exit the vehicle at
least three times. If nobody responds, officers should
approach the vehicle to clear the vehicle.

4. Clearing Vehicle

" At least two officers should be used to clear the subject
vehicle. The officers should approach the vehicle from an
angle with both officers on the same side of the vehicle.
The clearing officers should be as silent as possible so they
do not reveal their positions. The clearing officers should
slice the pie and clear the interior of the vehicle.

" Once the interior of the vehicle is cleared, the officers
should clear the trunk of the vehicle. One officer should
crouch at the rear of the vehicle, insert the key, and open
the trunk. The other officer should stand to the side and
rear of the trunk, with their firearm trained on the trunk.
Offices must be aware of crossfire when positioning themselves.
When the vehicle is completely cleared, this
information should be relayed to all other officers on the
scene.

F. Guidelines for Enforcement of Certain Traffic Violations

a. OWI Violations

1. See OWI Policy

b. Speeding Violations

1. Speed violations may be enforced by use of either radar, laser, or
vehicle paces with squad cars.

2. Officers conducting squad paces of speeding vehicles shall
attempt to pace the vehicle for approximately 1/10th mile while
neither gaining nor losing distance from the paced vehicle.

3. Squad paces resulting in enforcement action require the officer to
test the accuracy of the squad speedometer against police radar
or laser as soon as practical after the enforcement action, as
follows:
" The officer issuing the citation shall have another officer
set up and test a radar or laser unit.
" The arresting officer shall operate his/her squad through
the radar or laser zone and record the test results on the
back of the citation issued because of the squad's pace.
" The squad's speedometer shall be tested at the speed of
the violation and 10mph above and below the speed of
the violation.

4. General guidelines for speeding enforcement
" Speed violations should result in a written warning, or a
citation may be issued for such violations based on the
officer's discretion. Citation factors can include, but are
not limited to, road/weather conditions,
vehicle/pedestrian traffic conditions, complaints of speeding in the area, and the offender's prior driving
record, including prior warnings.
" Officers should vigorously enforce speed limits in school
zones at times when children are present. Speed
violations in a school zone when children are present
should generally result in the issuance of a traffic citation,
except in unusual circumstances.
" These guidelines are intended to guide officers in speeding
violation enforcement. The final determination of
whether a violation should result in a written warning or a
citation is left with the sound discretion of the officer
initiating the enforcement action based on all factors
known to the officer at the time of the traffic stop.

c. Equipment Violations

1. Violations of Chapter 347 under WI SS, Department of
Transportation Chapter TRANS 305, and Village ordinances
relating to vehicle equipment should be initially addressed with a
written corrective notice using a written warning through TraCS.

2. Officers may issue a written warning or traffic citation, at their
discretion, for modifications of vehicle equipment clearly in
violation of equipment laws or regulations.

3. Equipment repair orders that have not been satisfied shall be
returned to the issuing officer for follow-up investigation.
" Officers may re-contact the individual and provide
additional time to correct the violation.
" Individuals who fail to take corrective action once an
equipment warning has been issued may be issued a
citation addressing the proper violation.

4. When a business or privately-owned vehicle is the subject of an
equipment violation that is not corrected, the operator of the
vehicle at the time of the violation should be issued the citation
for the appropriate violation, not the business, business owner, or
private owner of the vehicle.

d. Public Carrier/Commercial Vehicle Violations

1. The enforcement of traffic laws applies equally to public carriers
and commercial vehicles.

2. Officers should attempt to expedite enforcement actions when
dealing with a public carrier so as not to unduly delay the
passengers.

3. Officers shall make a reasonable effort to ensure that valuable
cargo of commercial vehicles is protected, or arrangements are
made for passengers of public carriers if it becomes necessary to
temporarily detain the operator.

e. Multiple Violations

1. It is within the discretion of the investigating officer whether to
issue multiple citations for multiple violations from the same
incident.

2. As a general guideline, officers should issue a citation or citations
for the more serious offense(s) and give written warnings for the
lesser violations arising from the same incident.

3. Incidents involving multiple violations that constitute an all-
inclusive charge, such as eluding, OWI, or reckless driving, should
not result in individual charges for all violations when the greater
charge is also issued.

4. License and registration violations discovered during a traffic stop
for a moving violation, such as speeding or a stop sign violation,
may be charged in addition to the violation leading to the traffic
stop.

f. Other Hazardous Violations

1. Hazardous violations include, but are not limited to, offenses
involving excess speed, disregarding traffic control signs or
signals, alcohol offenses involving the use of a vehicle, reckless
driving, and attempting to elude an officer.

2. Officers should attempt to vigorously enforce traffic laws relating
to these types of violations.

g. Other Non-Hazardous Violations

1. Non-hazardous violations include, but are not limited to,
equipment violations, parking violations, operator licensing and
registration violations.

2. Officers should vigorously enforce these violations to address the
violations as well as create a public impression of active traffic law
enforcement activity to encourage voluntary compliance with all
traffic regulations.

h. Drivers License and Vehicle Registration Expirations

1. The department recognizes that expired vehicle registrations and
driver's licenses are often the result of mere oversight and not
intentional violations.

2. As a general guideline, officers should not issue a citation if a
vehicle registration or driver's license is expired for less than 30
days.

i. Newly Enacted Traffic Laws or Ordinances

1. Officers should use sound discretion when enforcing newly
enacted or amended traffic regulations.

2. For a period of 30 days after the enactment or major amendment
of a traffic law or regulation, officers should issue warnings for
violations if it appears the public may not be familiar with the new
law or amendment.

3. This section does not prevent an officer from taking more
stringent enforcement action if the officer is satisfied the offender
was aware of the new law or amendment and deliberately
violated the section, or if the violation is of such a hazardous
nature, stronger enforcement action is necessary to address the
violation.


G. Guidelines for Enforcement of Driver's License Violations

a. The driving status of all motorists stopped for any traffic or equipment
violation shall be checked at the time of the stop, assuming the DOT
Driver's Records are available, or as soon thereafter as possible.

b. Except in very unusual circumstances, a driver's status report of revoked,
suspended, cancelled, or no valid license issued, from the DOT Driver's
Records Files, coupled with the officer's observation of operation of a
vehicle, is sufficient probable cause to issue a citation for the appropriate
offense.

c. Officers shall not permit continued operation of the motor vehicle by a
driver cited for operating without a valid license, operating while
suspended, operating after revocation, or otherwise driving while
disqualified, but may permit operation by another person at the scene
who is validly licensed. The vehicle may be towed following the
guidelines in the Arrest Towing section of the TOW Policy. Officers shall
tow the vehicle if requested by the operator.

d. If the driver's status as a person can't be readily determined at the time
of the stop, either through DOT or departmental records, officers should
gather as much identifying information as possible and release the
operator, assuming no other violations requiring enforcement action are
present. If appropriate, officers should issue at least a department
warning form to document the stop and operation of the vehicle.
Subsequent determination of a revoked or suspended status shall result
in a follow-up investigation with appropriate enforcement action.

H. Radar and Laser Enforcement

a. Operational Procedures: Radar

1. Officers should choose locations having a high incidence of speed-
related crashes or speeding violations and under conditions
where the officer can properly observe traffic to confirm the
units readings by visual observation.

2. Before using the unit, officers shall perform the following
inspections and tests of the unit:

" A visual inspection of the radar unit shall be performed to
ensure there is no external damage, including frayed
power cords, to the unit.

" Perform internal calibration, light segment tests, and
external tuning fork tests in accordance with the
manufacturer's guidelines and specifications. These tests
shall also be conducted after each speeding citation is
issued, based on the use of the radar unit, and after radar
operation. All test results about a citation shall be
recorded in the narrative on the back of the citation or in
an original report.

3. Any external damage to the unit or failure of the unit to complete
all accuracy and calibration tests in accordance with the
manufacturer's specifications shall result in the removal of the
unit from use.

4. Officers who discover a malfunctioning unit or a unit with external
damage shall notify department supervision.

b. Radar and Laser Maintenance, and Calibration Records

1. It shall be the responsibility of the Chief of Police or his/her
designee to ensure all units used by the department meet
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration standards for
police radar and laser and are properly calibrated for use upon
receipt from the manufacturer.

2. All radar units shall be recalibrated by a qualified service
technician annually. A laser does not require any recalibration.

3. The Chief of Police or his/her designee shall be responsible for
ensuring all units are in proper working order and are repaired
and/or recalibrated as needed.

4. The Chief of Police or his/her designee shall be responsible for
maintaining all records of calibration and certification, repairs,
recalibration, and re-certification for departmental units.

c. Officer Radar and Laser Training and Certification

1. The Chief of Police shall ensure that all officers using the units are
properly trained and certified by the State of Wisconsin for the
use of police radar and laser.

2. The Chief of Police shall maintain all training records and records
of radar and laser certification for departmental personnel.

I. Driver Referral for Re-Examination

a. From time to time, officers will encounter people whose ability to
operate a motor vehicle is in question. This may be due to physical or
mental deficiencies, chronic use of alcohol or drugs, lack of knowledge of
traffic laws, or lack of driving skills.

b. Officers should be observant during routine traffic enforcement, crash
investigations, or any incident involving the use of a motor vehicle for
these individuals.

c. These people should be referred to the Department of Transportation for
reexamination by completing an incident report concerning the contact
and completion of a Driver Condition or Behavior Report to be sent to the
Department of Transportation.

d. This action should occur any time an officer questions the person's ability
to continue to operate a motor vehicle. It is not required that an officer
take enforcement action before referring a driver for reexamination. The
final determination of driving ability is left with the Department of
Transportation.

J. ALPR use

a. The use of any ALPR system, equipment, or data is restricted to authorized
police employees for official and legitimate law enforcement purposes and
enhancing public safety. Such use and goals include:

" Providing information to officers that will assist in ongoing
criminal investigations.
" Crime Prevention.
" Crime Detection
" The apprehension of wanted people.
" The identification of people who pose a safety threat to
the community.
" Ensuring the safety of vulnerable individuals through the
recovery of missing or endangered people.
" Improving the quality of life in our community through the
identification and removal of stolen vehicles.

b. Unofficial, improper, or otherwise unauthorized use of any ALPR system or
equipment, or unauthorized access, use, release, and/or dissemination of
ALPR data will be considered an infraction of department policy.

K. Use and Documentation of ALPR Date

" Access to stored ALPR data shall be limited to employees
designated by the administrator and issued a unique
individual log-in ID and password.
" Authorized employees may access stored ALPR data upon
a reasonable belief that the data is related to or useful as
part of a specific official action or investigation.
" When querying stored ALPR Data, the employee shall
include a case number whenever available and, under all
circumstances, add the purpose of the query in the
appropriate data field on the query screen.
" ALPR data is stored for 30 days; after that time, it is
automatically removed. The investigating officer/detective
must download any images or records needed for
evidentiary purposes within 30 days.

L. ALPR Audits

" The Lieutenant shall ensure an audit of the ALPR browsing
inquiries is conducted at least quarterly during each
calendar year.

M. Special Enforcement Procedures

a. Nonresident Traffic Violations

1. People receiving traffic citations for Village traffic ordinance or
state traffic forfeiture violations, who do not possess a valid
Wisconsin driver's license, or have sufficient ties to the
community, are subject to posting an appearance bond in cash at
the Cottage Grove Police Department.

" See OWI Policy for special release procedures.

2. Officers should offer every reasonable opportunity for people
identified in paragraph a., above, to contact someone to post bond on their behalf if they personally are unable to do so. If a
person is unable to post the bond, s/he may be incarcerated at the Dane County Jail until the bond is posted or until a bond
appearance can be made in court.

b. Juvenile Traffic Offenders

1. See ARREST and JUVENILE Policies.

c. Foreign Diplomats, Officials, and Foreign Nationals

1. Officers who encounter a person who claims diplomatic immunity
from arrest, either personally or as a family member, employee,
or servant of a diplomatic mission, shall immediately notify a
supervisor.

2. Officers shall treat these individuals with courtesy and refrain
from physically restraining or handcuffing these individuals unless
officer or citizen safety considerations require this action.

3. The supervisor shall determine the appropriate action to be taken
with respect to the person claiming diplomatic immunity.

4. The incident shall be fully documented, regardless of the
underlying nature of the incident, by the investigation officer in an
incident report, including a narrative describing the details and
circumstances of the contact.

5. Officers who detain or arrest people who identify themselves as
foreign nationals shall notify a supervisor of such status as soon as
possible. The supervisor shall make the necessary notifications to
the embassy or consulate of the country concerned.

6. Officers who detain or arrest people who identify themselves as
legislators shall notify their on-duty supervisor of such status as
soon as possible. Officers shall deal with people identifying
themselves as legislators as they would any other citizen. The
incident shall be fully documented, regardless of the underlying
nature of the incident, by the investigating officer in an incident
report, including a narrative describing the details and
circumstances of the contact.

d. Military Personnel

1. Military personnel, for purposes of this policy, are active-duty
members of the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines, Space Force, or
Coast Guard, or any member of the Reserve Components or
National Guard on active-duty orders.

2. If an active duty member of the armed forces, or a civilian
employee of the military acting within the scope of their
employment, is involved in a crash resulting in death, or injury
requiring hospitalization, and military authorities have not been
notified by other means, the officer shall notify the military law
enforcement authorities of the nearest active duty military
installation of the person's branch of service and apprise them of
the incident.

3. If a Reservist or National Guardsman on active-duty orders, or
while performing any military duties, including weekend drills, is
injured or killed and notification is required as in paragraph b.,
above, the individual's Reserve or National Guard unit or the
nearest Reserve Center or National Guard Armory shall be
notified.

4. All active-duty military personnel who possess a valid Wisconsin
driver's license, or who are assigned to military installations within
the State of Wisconsin, even if a legal resident of another state,
shall be considered residents of this state for purposes of
requiring the posting of a bond.

N. General and Selective Traffic Law Enforcement

a. Officers are encouraged to initiate traffic law enforcement patrol
practices involving area or line patrol techniques and stationary
observations of traffic conditions. These highly visible patrol techniques
are the greatest single deterrent to traffic violations for the average
motorist.

b. The Chief of Police or designee shall perform an analysis of the traffic
crash and traffic enforcement summaries supplied by the Support
Services Manager.

1. See TRADMIN Policy.

c. The analysis should include geographic, temporal, and causative factor
considerations for vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian crashes and violations.
Based on this analysis, the Chief of Police or designee shall develop
selective enforcement programs for their teams using the following
criteria:

1. Patrol personnel shall be deployed to those areas and at those
times when the analysis shows high rates of crashes and/or traffic
violations occur. The selective enforcement program should
consider bicycle and pedestrian crashes and violations, as well as
incorporate efforts to reduce these incidents, including public
education efforts.

2. The type of selective enforcement countermeasures should be
based on human, vehicle, and environmental factors leading to
crashes and violations.

3. The type of selective enforcement practices; area, line, or directed
patrol; covert or overt stationary observation; or the use of
marked or unmarked vehicles shall be at the discretion of the
Chief of Police or designee to monitor the selective enforcement
activity.

4. While the use of marked patrol vehicles in either moving or visible
stationary assignments has the greatest deterrent effect on
motorists, the Chief of Police or designee may assign unmarked
vehicles or covertly positioned vehicles for traffic enforcement
activities. These assignments should be limited to situations
where the effectiveness of the enforcement action would be
enhanced using unmarked or covert observation due to the type
of violation or the geographic location where the enforcement
action is taking place.

5. All patrol vehicles, including unmarked vehicles, used for traffic
enforcement, shall have operational red and/or red and blue
emergency vehicle lights and a siren.

d. Selective enforcement programs will be analyzed and/or reviewed as
needed, but at a minimum, these programs will be evaluated at least
annually by the Chief of Police or designee.

O. Bicycle and Pedestrian Enforcement Activities

a. All officers should be familiar with Village ordinances and state traffic
regulations relating to bicycles and pedestrians.

b. Juvenile violators of bicycle and/or pedestrian regulations may be dealt
with in the following manner at the officer's discretion:

1. Give a verbal warning.

2. Juveniles, at least 12 years of age, may be issued a Village
ordinance violation citation for a violation of the Village
ordinances relating to violations.

" See JUVENILE Policy.

c. Any type of enforcement action listed in paragraphs 2 a-c, above, may be
selected by officers for adults who violate traffic laws or ordinances.

d. If a violation involves a lack of required safety equipment or lighting
equipment at night, the officer may direct the cyclist to dismount and
walk the bicycle to their destination. If pedestrians are not endangered,
the officer may permit the use of sidewalks for riding purposes to the
bicyclist's destination.

P. Off-Road Vehicle Traffic Enforcement Activities
a. General traffic enforcement and selective traffic enforcement programs
for patrol teams shall consider and include efforts to reduce crashes and
violations involving the use of off-road vehicles, including minibikes,
snowmobiles, UTVs, and all-terrain vehicles.

b. Emphasis in these programs should include:

1. Public education efforts to include safe operation as well as the
legal requirements of operation.
2. Licensing, registration, and equipment violations.
3. Illegal operation on roadways.
4. Illegal operation on public or private property.

IX. AUTOMATED LICENSE PLATE RECOGNITION (ALPR)

Chapter 19.3  Patrol  Equipment


Purpose

The purpose of this policy is to establish comprehensive guidelines governing the use, operation, and

management of the Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) systems by the department. This policy is

designed to ensure that all deployment and utilization of ALPR technology is conducted in strict compliance with

Virginia state laws and regulations, particularly those concerning privacy, data retention, and lawful criminal

justice practices. The policy also promotes the effective and responsible use of ALPR systems in support of public

safety efforts and criminal investigations, while protecting individual rights.



Policy Statement



The department shall operate its ALPR systems exclusively for legitimate law enforcement purposes. These

include, but are not limited to, locating stolen vehicles or license plates, identifying vehicles associated with

missing persons or wanted individuals, supporting active criminal investigations, and responding to alerts from

official notifications such as AMBER and SILVER Alerts or terrorist watch lists.

Under no circumstances will ALPR technology be used to monitor constitutionally protected activities, target

individuals based on their speech, or interfere with lawful public behavior. Any unauthorized use or sharing of

ALPR data is strictly prohibited and may result in disciplinary action or criminal penalties under the laws of the

Commonwealth of Virginia.

The Department is committed to providing transparency in our use of ALPR systems by providing a dedicated

Transparency Portal webpage along with providing public education through engagement and the use of social

media platforms.

The Department is committed to following the Code of Virginia �2.2-5517, as amended, which became effective

on July 1, 2025. All officers shall be familiar with this Code and follow it at all times.



Definitions

Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR)  Technology that utilizes high-speed cameras and specialized

software to capture and convert images of vehicle license plates into machine-readable data.

" Hit or Notification  Occurs when the system identifies a license plate that matches a record from an

authorized database or hot list.

" Hot list  Is a collection of license plates associated with criminal activity or public safety concerns, such

as those from the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) or Virginia Criminal Information Network (VCIN).

The department may also develop a Custom Hot List for vehicles under specific local investigation.

" Query  Refers to a user-initiated search of ALPR data.

" Audit trail  A system-generated log that documents all access and queries, including user credentials,

date and time, the license plate queried, the stated purpose, and any related case number.

" LPR Administrator  Is the person(s) designated to oversee and manage the departments ALPR program.

" Law-enforcement agency  Any agency defined under � 9.1-101 of the Code of Virginia.



System Requirements

All ALPR systems deployed by the Department must adhere to specific technical and security standards. Each

vendor must certify in writing that they will not sell or share any system or audit data without the departments

request or consent. System data must be automatically purged after 21 days unless linked to an active criminal

investigation. Audit trail data must be retained for two years, unless a longer retention period is legally

mandated.





Additionally, all systems must conform to the standards set by the Virginia Information Technologies Agency

(VITA), and approved by the Division of Purchases and Supply of the Department of General Services. Databases

used by ALPR systems for notification purposes must be updated at least every 24 hours to ensure accuracy.



Permissible Uses

The use of ALPR systems by the Department shall be limited strictly to approved law enforcement functions.

These include:

" Criminal investigations involving violations of Virginia law or local ordinances where reasonable suspicion

exist;

" Locating missing, endangered, or abducted individuals (Amber and Silver Alerts);

" Responding to alerts related to outstanding warrants, stolen vehicles or plates, and human trafficking

investigations;

" ALPR may also support traffic enforcement activities, provided such use is consistent with state law and

internal department policy.

Data Retention and Sharing

In accordance with state law, ALPR system data shall be retained for no longer than 21 days unless the data are

linked to an ongoing criminal investigation. Audit trail records shall be preserved for two years unless otherwise

required by law.

ALPR data are not subject to public disclosure under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). Sharing of

ALPR data is restricted to authorized parties, which include other law enforcement agencies, Commonwealths

Attorneys, defense attorneys pursuant to court order, and courts responding to subpoenas or legal requests.

Any unauthorized access or distribution of ALPR data is prohibited and punishable under Virginia law.

In accordance with state law, the department will not share system data with any agency outside the

Commonwealth of Virginia.

The Department will comply with all reporting requirements of the Virginia State Crime Commission.



Operational Procedures

ALPR units may be deployed on a permanent or temporary basis, but must receive prior approval from the Chief

of Police. Only VCIN-certified personnel who are specifically authorized may access ALPR systems. All access

must occur using individualized login credentials, and permissions must be limited according to the employees

job assignment. Officers are required to log into the ALPR system at the beginning of their shift.

When the ALPR system generates a hit, the officer must visually verify that the observed license plate matches

the system notification. The officer shall confirm license plate of the alert through the NCIC or VCIN database

through the Culpeper County Emergency Communications Center (ECC). A hit from the ALPR system alone does

not constitute reasonable suspicion for enforcement action; confirmation is mandatory.

Hits associated with terrorist watch lists or violent gang databases are to be treated as informational alerts

only, not immediate cause for enforcement.

Investigative Use and Responsibilities

Custom hot list entries must be reviewed and approved by a LPR Administrator or a Supervisor before being

entered into the ALPR system. These entries must be promptly removed once they are no longer relevant to an

active investigation. Investigating officers are responsible for ensuring that any custom entries remain accurate

and necessary. The use of custom hot lists does not replace mandatory NCIC or VCIN entry requirements for

wanted or missing persons.



Training and System Security

All personnel who operate or access ALPR systems must complete training in addition to maintaining current

VCIN certification. The LPR Administrator, in collaboration with the Training Unit, shall coordinate and document

all training activities. Internal department procedures shall prohibit downloading or retaining unrelated ALPR

data, require regular database updates, ensure system access is restricted to authorized personnel, and outline

secure storage and proper destruction of data.

The LPR Administrator shall conduct an internal auditing procedure that occurs at least once every 30 days.

Reporting Requirements

The department shall submit an annual report to the Virginia Department of State Police detailing the number

of ALPR cameras deployed, the specific databases used for notifications, the total number of queries performed

and their purposes, and the demographic data of identified suspects and drivers stopped. The report shall also

include the number of vehicle stops resulting from ALPR hits, any incidents of unauthorized access or misuse,

and legal requests received for system data, including subpoenas, warrants, or Subpoena Duces Tecums.



Public Awareness and Transparency

To foster transparency and public trust, the department will publish this ALPR policy on its official website. The

Department will also release the ALPR data in its annual report, excluding any personal information or sensitive

case details that would compromise ongoing investigations or violate individual privacy rights.

Additionally, the Department will maintain a Transparency Portal website where anyone can view:

" Department policy;

" Review a list of law enforcement agencies where ALPR data is shared;

" Aggregate number of vehicles captured in the prior 30 days;

" Number of hot list hits the past 30 days;

" And the number of queries in the last 30 days.

The Transparency Portal website can be located at:

https://transparency.flocksafety.com/culpeper-va-pd-



Prohibited Uses

Under no circumstances may ALPR systems be used to monitor individuals based on their constitutionally

protected speech or legal activities. The department strictly prohibits using the system for any type of

surveillance without a clear legal basis, or for any form of data mining or information gathering that is not

directly connected to a criminal justice purpose.

Any individual who willfully misuses the ALPR system, or who unlawfully accesses or shares data from the

system, shall be subject to enforcement under Virginia law. Violations may result in Class 1 misdemeanor

charges, the exclusion of improperly obtained evidence from judicial proceedings, and internal disciplinary

actions, up to and including termination.



Policy Exemptions

This policy does not apply to ALPR systems that are operated by the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles

(DMV), traffic enforcement systems not related to criminal investigation, or to other non-criminal justice

applications managed by government entities outside the department.



Permits and Legal Compliance

Before installing ALPR equipment on state-maintained property, the department shall obtain all required

permits from the Town of Culpeper Zoning Department. Vendors contracted to provide ALPR technology must

notify the department immediately upon receiving any legal request for system data, including subpoenas or

search warrants.



By following this policy, the department ensures that its ALPR program is used lawfully, transparently, and

responsibly, in alignment with state laws and departmental standards. This policy is intended to protect the

privacy rights of the public while enhancing the departments ability to safeguard the community and respond

effectively to crime.

25EP41039 to Flock ALPR Notification Leads to Narcotics Arrest
elmira-city-ny-pd:
On December 11, 2025, Flock Safety cameras alerted Elmira Police to a stolen vehicle traveling through the city. Officers located the vehicle parked near a residence and coordinated surveillance until it began moving again.

Officers conducted a controlled high-risk stop, safely detaining all occupants. A subsequent investigation confirmed the vehicle was stolen from another jurisdiction. Officers also seized multiple quantities of suspected fentanyl and methamphetamine during the arrest.

The primary suspect admitted to the vehicle theft and was charged accordingly. The vehicle was recovered and evidence was secured for prosecution. This case demonstrates how license plate reader technology supports proactive policing, removes illegal drugs from circulation, and helps recover stolen property while prioritizing safety and accountability.

column1: 25EP38220 to Flock Alert Leads to Stolen Vehicle Recovery
elmira-city-ny-pd:
On November 15, 2025, Flock Safety cameras alerted Elmira Police to a stolen vehicle traveling within the city. Patrol officers located the vehicle shortly afterward and coordinated a high-risk traffic stop with multiple units present to ensure safety.

The occupants were detained without incident, and the vehicle was confirmed stolen from another state. After coordinating with the originating agency, the vehicle was impounded and secured so it could be returned to its owner.

This case highlights how license plate reader technology supports proactive policing, enhances officer and public safety, and improves inter-agency cooperation in recovering stolen vehicles.

column1: Balsam Street Shooting Investigation
elmira-city-ny-pd:
On March 15th 2025 at 01:35am, Elmira Police Officers were dispatched to Balsam St near
Broadway St for reported gun shots. No individuals were known to have been injured or struck by
gunfire. Notification of the shooting had been received by the Chemung County E-911
Communications Center via the Flock Raven acoustic gunshot detection system. While responding to
the location, it was learned that an involved vehicle was fleeing the area at a high rate of speed. An
Elmira Police Officer subsequently located the fleeing vehicle near Broadway St and South Ave and
three people were taken into custody.
Investigators with the Elmira Police Department Detective Bureau and the Gun Involved Violence

Elimination (G.I.V.E.) Initiative Unit were summoned to the scene to assist. A defaced 9mm semi-
automatic handgun and spent shell casings were recovered and an arrest has been made.

Jaheim Brown, a 23-year-old Elmira resident has been charged with Criminal Possession of a
Weapon in the Second Degree; loaded firearm, a class C felony, and Criminal Possession of a
Weapon in the Third Degree; defaced firearm, a class D felony. Jaheim Brown remains in the
custody of the Elmira Police Department pending formal arraignment in Elmira City Court.
The Elmira Police Department would like to thank the Chemung County E-911 Communications
Center, the Chemung County Sheriffs Office, and the New York State Police for their assistance in
this investigation.
The Elmira Police Department is asking anyone with information about this matter to call the
Elmira Police Department at (607)737-5626 or leave a message on the anonymous tip-line at
(607)271-HALT.

column1: 25EP39623 to Police Dispatched to Shooting Despite no 911 caller(s)
elmira-city-ny-pd:
On November 29, 2025, Elmira Police were alerted to possible gunfire through the Flock Raven acoustic gunshot detection system. Notably, no 911 calls were received reporting shots fired at the time of the incident. The Raven alert was the sole reason officers were dispatched to the area.

Officers responded immediately and located spent shell casings in the roadway, confirming that a shooting had occurred. Further investigation revealed that a nearby residence had been struck by multiple rounds. Officers made contact with occupants, conducted a safety check of the home, and confirmed that no one was injured.



Evidence was recovered and secured, and the shooter was subsequently identified and arrested. This event demonstrates how Flock Raven technology can detect and alert police to gunfire that may otherwise go unreported, allowing officers to respond quickly, check on residents safety, and preserve evidence even when no one calls 911.

column1: 25EP01938 to Flock Raven Alert Leads Police to Ballistic Evidence
elmira-city-ny-pd:
On January 19, 2025, Elmira Police were dispatched to the area of Clemens Center Parkway at Penn Ave following an alert from the Flock Raven acoustic gunshot detection system. No 911 calls were received reporting shots fired; the Raven alert was the only notification of the incident.

Officers responded promptly and located a spent shell casing in the area, confirming that a shooting had occurred. On a later date, a person was arrested in possession of a firearm.

That firearm was test-fired and submitted for analysis. Through NIBIN ballistic analysis conducted at the DCJS Southern Tier Satellite Crime Lab, the recovered firearm was forensically linked to the earlier shooting incident.

This case demonstrates how Flock Raven technology can identify otherwise unreported gunfire, allowing officers to respond quickly, recover ballistic evidence, and use forensic tools to connect firearms to violent incidentsstrengthening investigations and accountability.

prince-george-county-va-pd: Before sunrise recently, a cyclist equipped with proper lighting was struck from behind by a vehicle that fled the scene. The collision left the cyclist with significant injuries. While investigators found no license plate at the scene, they recovered broken mirror fragments that identified the vehicle's likely make and model. santa-rosa-ca-pd:
ALPR Technology Leads to Identification of Suspect Responsible for Multiple Armed Robberies
Between January 10 and January 15, 2026, four armed robberies and attempted robberies at local gas stations were reported to the Santa Rosa Police Department (SRPD). In each of the incidents, the suspect was described as an adult male wearing a face mask, dark clothing, and carrying what appeared to be a rifle and had fled the area before police arrival. On the morning of January 15, following the two most recent robbery attempts, detectives with the SRPD Violent Crimes Team were able to identify Damian Garza, a 23-year-old resident of Santa Rosa, as the suspect in these incidents using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) technology.
On January 10, at approximately 7:30 p.m., officers responded to an armed robbery at a Valero gas station at 1101 Yulupa Avenue. The suspect, described as adult male, wearing a black puffy jacket, black shorts, and a mask, entered the business, brandished a rifle, and demanded cash from the clerk. The suspect fled the area with an undisclosed amount of cash.
On January 13, at approximately 7:20 p.m., officers were dispatched to the Valero gas station at 1333 4th Street for an attempted armed robbery. An adult male, wearing a black hooded jacket, black pants, and wearing a mask entered the store and brandished what appeared to be a rifle and demanded cash. The clerk was able to run outside, at which point the suspect also fled the store without any money or merchandise.
On January 15, at approximately 4:13 a.m., officers were dispatched to the Shell gas station at 255 Dutton Avenue to investigate an alarm call. Upon arrival, officers learned an adult male, wearing dark clothing and a face covering entered the store with what appeared to be a rifle or shotgun concealed under his jacket. After being refused the contents of the cash register drawer, the suspect left the store without any money or merchandise.
At approximately 6:37 a.m. on January 15, officers were dispatched to the Valero gas stations at 1101 Yulupa Avenue for a report of an armed robbery, the second at this location in five days. The suspect in this incident was wearing clothing similar to the clothing worn during the previous attempted robbery at the Shell station. A rifle or shotgun was seen under his jacket. The suspect fled the area with an undisclosed amount of cash and merchandise.
No customers were present during any of these incidents, and no gas station employees were injured. The suspect(s) and firearm(s) used in these incidents remain outstanding.
In each of these incidents, the suspect was able to flee the area prior to the arrival of officers. Extensive searches were conducted, each with negative results. Detectives with the SRPD Violent Crimes Investigations teams, believing these incidents likely involved the same masked suspect, utilized vehicle data captured by fixed ALPR cameras near the locations of the gas stations. SRPD uses fixed Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras to help investigate serious crimes. These cameras capture license plates, vehicle descriptions, and time-and-location data, allowing detectives to quickly identify and track suspect vehicles involved in crimes such as robberies.
Detectives located a grey Acura sedan that was in the area of each of the gas stations at times consistent with the robberies and attempted robberies. Using the license plate captured by the cameras, detectives were able to quickly associate Garza with the vehicle.Detectives located the vehicle at Garzas residence in the 2200 block of Midway Drive. When Garza exited his residence and got into the vehicle, they noted he was of a similar physical build and dressed in similar clothing as the suspect in the investigations earlier in the morning. Detectives followed Garza as he drove away from the residence, and at approximately 9:15 a.m., two uniformed officers with the SRPD Downtown Enforcement Team conducted a traffic stop on Garzas vehicle. Garza was detained without incident.
At approximately 1:30 p.m., detectives served a search warrant at Garzas house on Midway Drive. During the search warrant, detectives located clothing consistent with each of the robberies, merchandise believed to have been stolen from one of the gas stations, and a pellet rifle.
As the investigation continued, detectives were able to connect Garza to an unsolved robbery in December 2025. On December 16, at approximately 9:00 p.m., Garza robbed the Valero gas station located at 1101 Yulupa Avenue. He was wearing dark clothing and a Halloween mask. No weapon was seen and no threats of a weapon were made. Garza fled the gas station with an undisclosed amount of cash.
Garza was booked into Sonoma County Jail for five counts of robbery per 211 PC.
ALPR technology is a critical tool in reducing and solving violent crimes by providing real-time data that helps identify suspect vehicles and generate actionable leads within minutes. This capability not only accelerates investigations but also prevents dangerous encounters by allowing officers to intercept suspects before violence escalates. This innovation reflects SRPDs commitment to leveraging technology for faster response times, smarter resource deployment, and violent crime reduction, ensuring a safer Santa Rosa.

fort-collins-co-pd: A hotlist is a defined list of license plates that the LPR system checks against; when a vehicle captured by a Flock LPR camera matches an entry on a hotlist, the system generates an LPR alert to authorized Flock users.

Organizations with access to FCPS data
fort-collins-co-pd:
FCPS securely shares license plate reader data with select law enforcement partners for legitimate public safety purposes. The agencies listed below have been granted permission by FCPS to search LPR data captured by our cameras.


LPR data is owned by FCPS and is never sold to third parties. LPR data includes the image of the back of the vehicle, the license plate, and the date, time, and location that it passed the camera. Outside agencies cannot access our data unless FCPS has explicitly granted them access through our sharing settings. These agencies will only see data collected by our cameras if they perform a specific search, and a vehicle with the searched-for plate number or description has driven past one of our cameras in the last 30 days. All searches and the purpose for the search is recorded in our audit logs. If any search is conducted with a purpose related to immigration enforcement or reproductive care, all data collected by FCPS cameras is automatically removed from the search and inaccessible to the searcher. Sharing relationships can be revoked at any time. column1: Recent Success Story #1
glastonbury-ct-pd: Case #2600001827 On 1/20/26 at approximately 0351 hrs GPD received an LPR hit on a vehicle stolen out of Greenwich that was traveling on Glastonbury Blvd. Officers located the vehicle in the lot of Cumberland Farms and detained the operator. Officers discovered that there was another vehicle traveling in tandem with the reported stolen vehicle. Officers learned that this second vehicle was a not yet reported stolen vehicle, as it was taken overnight and the owner was unaware it had been taken. Both vehicle operators were placed under arrest.
sioux-city-ia-pd:
Runaway Juvenile Safely Recovered

When a juvenile ran away from a foster home and was believed to be with their birth mother, investigators used social media images to narrow down the type of vehicle involved. After identifying the mothers Mazda and entering its plate into the Flock system, officers received an alert when the vehicle was detected out of state. This information allowed law enforcement to quickly locate the vehicle and safely recover the missing juvenile. The birth mother, who had repeatedly denied knowing the juveniles whereabouts, was later charged with Harboring a Runaway Child.

column1: Recent Success Story #2
glastonbury-ct-pd: Case #2500035656 11/29/25 Received an LPR hit on a stolen vehicle on Hebron Ave. Suspect vehicle was located in a nearby apartment complex while it's occupants were attempting to steal a second vehicle. Multiple suspects fled on foot and were quickly apprehended by patrol officers.
sioux-city-ia-pd:
Arson and Homicide Suspect Tracked Across State Lines

A suspect, angry with an ex-girlfriend, set a fire in her apartment and later the same day opened fire on two pedestrians, killing one. The suspect fled across state lines and was considered armed and extremely dangerous. Using Flock license plate recognition data, investigators were able to build a clear timeline of the suspect vehicles movements, placing it in the area at the time of both the arson and the homicide. When the vehicle was later spotted and a pursuit ensued, the car crashed into a pole and the suspect surrendered. The individual was charged with Murder 1st, Arson 1st, Domestic Assault, and additional offenses, and the weapon was recovered without further harm to officers or the public.

column1: Recent Success Story #3
glastonbury-ct-pd: Case #2500033725 11/6/25 Received an LPR hit on a stolen vehicle/overdue rental vehicle. Officers located the vehicle in the lot of a bank, at which time two individuals walked out of the bank and attempted to enter the vehicle. Both were detained and it was determined that they had attempted to fraudulently withdraw money from an account that did not belong to them inside of the bank. Search of the vehicle revealed numerous forged/counterfeit identity documents and narcotics.
sioux-city-ia-pd:
Mail Theft and Check Forgery Ring Disrupted

Residents reported a suspect stealing outgoing mail from a neighborhood mailbox, and a home security camera captured the suspect and vehicle. Detectives used the video to determine the make, model, color, and state on the license plate, then entered that information into Flock. The system returned an exact plate, which was shared with officers in the field. Shortly afterward, the suspect vehicle was stopped and multiple individuals were detained. Inside the vehicle, officers found numerous stolen and forged checks and mail taken from several locations across Sioux City, including an entire apartment building. The suspects, who were from out of state and previously unknown to local officers, were identified and face charges including Theft, Forgery, and Criminal Mischief thanks to the Flock-assisted traffic stop.

glastonbury-ct-pd: Case #2500030968 10/5/25 Responded to a vehicle burglary at the Riverfront Community Center in which a victims purse was stolen and her checks were fraudulently cashed. Investigators were able to view surveillance footage of the suspect vehicle, which was then compared to LPR captures, at which point the vehicles registration was determined. As a result of the LPR and further investigative measures in collaboration with numerous other agencies who experienced similar felony lane gang style thefts, suspects have been identified and warrants are pending.

FAQ
heath-tx-dps:
1. Are these cameras just a way for the government to track innocent people everywhere they go?

Response: No. Flock cameras do not track people; they capture license plates. The system is not facial recognition, it does not know who is driving, and it cannot identify passengers. The data is used for specific criminal investigations, not general surveillance. Without an active law enforcement case, officers do not pull or review the data.

2. How do we know the cameras won't be abused?

Response: In Heath, access is strictly limited, every search is logged, and improper use would be grounds for immediate discipline or termination. Just like we hold officers accountable for misuse of other sensitive systems (like TCIC/NCIC or body-worn cameras), there are clear checks and audits to prevent abuse. Officers found to misuse the technology are subject to disciplinary action, up to termination.

3. What happens if the system makes a mistake and misreads a plate?

Response: Mistakes can happen with any technology, but officers are trained that an alert is just an alert, not proof. Every Flock hit must be confirmed by the officer visually matching the license plate and vehicle description before any action is taken. A misread plate alone cannot justify a stop.

4. Isn't this just constant mass surveillance of everyone in the city?

Response: The system does not create a permanent database of every car and every trip. Data is automatically deleted after a set retention period (30 days unless part of an active investigation). Unlike private companies that can hold onto your information indefinitely, our use of the system is governed by policy, retention limits, and accountability.

5. What about the argument that other cities have canceled its program after poor results?

Response: Different cities see different results based on how they implement the program. In Heath, we are a smaller, growing city with high traffic from surrounding communities. Our system has already produced recoveries of stolen vehicles, and arrests of violent wanted people. Unlike some cities where millions of plates are scanned daily, our scale and use are tailored to local needs.

6. Isn't this giving too much power to a private company like Flock Safety?

Response: Flock provides the technology, but the City of Heath owns the data. The company cannot sell or use it for commercial purposes. It is only accessible to trained law enforcement personnel and is governed by strict contracts and department policy.

7. Why should citizens accept this when private misuse has happened elsewhere?

Response: It's important to understand that license plate checks already happen outside law enforcement. Retailers like Lowe's and Home Depot use Flock on their property to reduce theft. Towing companies and repossession services run records through DMV and other systems every day. What the City of Heath provides is actually more regulated and more accountable than what many private businesses already do.

8. Does this system really make us safer?

Response: Yes. Flock cameras are proven tools in helping police solve crimes faster. They have been used to recover stolen vehicles, locate missing children, and even identify suspects fleeing from violent crimes. In public safety, even one prevented tragedy or one recovered child makes the investment worthwhile.

9. Is this technology replacing traditional police work?

Response: No. The cameras are not a substitute for officers, investigations, or community engagement. They are simply one more tool like radios, body cameras, or 911 dispatch systems that help officers work more effectively. Police work is still done by people, with accountability and oversight.

10. How can citizens trust that their privacy is protected?

Response: Trust comes from transparency and oversight. Our policy is public, our use is auditable, and data is retained only for a short period. If a citizen has a concern, we can show the safeguards in place. We welcome those conversations because accountability is part of building trust.
