column1: Hopewell PD's ALPR Policy
hopewell-va-pd:
General Order OPR 02-12 FLOCK LPR Systems

Purpose: The use of License Plate Recognition (LPR) Equipment is intended
to provide sworn law enforcement personnel with an automated
method of identifying vehicles and license plates that have a
specific interest to law enforcement. The use of LPR equipment
shall be limited to law enforcement purposes only and deployed in
a manner consistent with this policy.

I. Definitions

A. FLOCK Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) Falcon System-
Equipment consisting of fixed location camera(s), a central processing unit

(CPU), camera/power/data wires, and software used to automatically send a
data signal to an off-site server, recognize and interpret the characters on vehicle
license plates, and vehicle descriptors (color, style, make, model). This data is
then compared against a known list of license plates bearing some significance
to law enforcement.
B. Hot List- A database populated with items of specific concern to the investigative
and/or enforcement interests of law enforcement in the City of Hopewell. This
may include, but is not limited to, Terrorist Screening Center (TSC) watch lists,
sex offender registry, stolen/wanted vehicles, and license plates, wanted and
missing persons, cautions, and license plates associated with Amber Alerts or
various watch lists provided for law enforcement purposes.

07-10.2

C. Download- Transfer of data from the Virginia State Police database consisting of
license plate-associated data. This download is done automatically through the
FLOCK LPR off-site servers.
D. Notifications- Also known as a HIT. A positive indication notification, by
email/text/app, is a potential match between data on the HOT LIST and a license
plate scanned by the LPR system. A hit IS NOT conclusive confirmation that a
license plate is wanted and additional investigation is ALWAYS warranted when
a hit is indicated.
E. LPR Generated Data- All information, including location, date, and time of a
license plate encounter and any LPR-generated digital photographic image(s) of
the license plate and vehicle generated entirely through the use of/and by the
LPR equipment.
F. LPR Coordinator- Designee in the department responsible for managing LPR
users. Responsibilities include instructing individual users on the proper
procedures for operating the LPR software, and adding and removing authorized
users to the server. Ensures that users are updating the electronic Hot List and
entries are up to date on a regular basis. The Support Services Commander will
be the agencys primary LPR coordinator.

II. Procedures
A. LPR Users
1. All users shall receive training from the LPR coordinator or designee
prior to using the LPR system.
2. It shall be the responsibility of each LPR user to verify the most current
Hot List.
3. ALPR Hits do not, by themselves, constitute reasonable suspicion for
a vehicular stop. Upon receiving a notification, the user should
determine the accuracy of the Hit. The LPR user will visually verify that
the actual vehicle tag and the read on the LPR screen are the same
(same state, same numerical/alphabetic characters).
4. The user will confirm the Hit is currently active by running the
information through NCIC/VCIN.
5. The user will ensure that they are in a position to safely determine the

07-10.3

accuracy of the Hit in accordance with department policy OPR 01-01
Emergency Vehicle Operations.
6. Additional information may be entered into the LPR system at any time.
Broadcast information received during a tour of duty should be manually
entered immediately upon receipt by the LPR user. The reason for the
entry should be noted in the entry screen (i.e. stolen vehicle, missing
person, abduction, Amber Alert, robbery suspect, etc), as well as the
case number (if the incident occurred in Hopewell), the date of entry,
and contact information for the entering officer.
7. Upon completing a manual entry, the user should query the LPR data to
determine if the license plate was scanned previously. Users are
required to remove Hot List entries at the completion of their
investigation.

8. Users may access data when investigating any specific law-
enforcement purpose where the data may be able to provide suspect

information. Data can be searched and filtered based on vehicle type,
camera location, and date/time. All searches of data will require a
search reason. Officers shall use the full CAD event/report number (if
available) or related nature (shots fired, stolen vehicle, crime solvers tip,
etc.) as their search reason.

III. Data Retention, Access, and Dissemination

1. Access to the Falcon LPR systems is achieved through individualized login to
Flocks web-based server. Once logged in, officers will be able to receive hot
list alerts within the system and can view and search data. Officers will be
required to enter a search reason for auditing purposes.
2. Flock is Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) compliant, and all
information is encrypted at rest in the cloud using Amazon Web Services
(AWS) Key Management Service (KMS) Keys, which use Federal Information
Processing Standards (FIPS) 140-2 validated hardware security modules to
generate and store the keys. All logins and queries will be stored and
monitored including:
a. Username
b. Date
c. Time
d. Purpose of query
e. License plate and other elements used to query the system.
3. Flock Group Inc., the ALPR vendor, will store the data (data hosting) and

07-10.4

ensure proper maintenance and security of data stored in their cloud-based
system. Flock will also oversee purging data at the end of the 21-day storage
period. Users are responsible for extracting, downloading, and archiving
footage from Flock on its own storage devices for auditing, prosecutorial, and
administrative purposes.
4. The LPR System Coordinator is responsible for the management of user
accounts. Authorized users shall be limited to current employees who are
legally authorized to review LPR data for crime prevention and detection
purposes.
5. Each authorized user agrees that LPR-generated data, Hot List information,
and, networking resources are to be used solely for law enforcement
purposes only and consistent with the law. Authorized users shall not use or
share the information for any unethical, illegal, or criminal purpose. Under no
circumstances shall officers share LPR data with any non-law enforcement
agency or out of state law enforcement agency. Any requests for LPR
information from a non-law enforcement agency shall be forwarded to the
office of the Chief of Police or his designee.
6. ALPR data is considered a record of a criminal investigation and is
confidential and not a public record. Data shall not be disclosed outside of the
Hopewell Police Department except for safety purposes pursuant to a written
or electronic request from another requesting law-enforcement agency. The
request must indicate the agencys incident number and why the agency is
requesting the APLR data, i.e., missing person, wanted subject, stolen
vehicle, etc. Any Flock system administrator (Lieutenant and above) can
authorize to release of the requested information after reviewing and
approving the request.
7. On a daily basis, The ALPR Coordinator shall ensure the current Hot List
from the Virginia State Police Fusion Center has been updated through the
automatic interface. The hotlist will be update at a minimum once every 24
hours or as soon a practicable per the code of Virginia, � 2.2-5517
8. LPR users shall not access information in an LPR system by using a name or
password that was assigned to another person, including another user.
9. All FOIA requests for ALPR data (if available) will be submitted and evaluated
through the City of Hopewell Attorneys Office.

results of their annual reports.

Missing Person
Protection Order
Immigration Violation
Sex Offender

Internal Affairs will audit these searches every six months and will prepare a report for the Chief of Police.

On December 20, 2025, Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) technology helped the Quincy Police Department quickly recover a stolen vehicle and return personal property to its rightful owner.
At 4:36 p.m., the police received an ALPR alert about a stolen 2001 Mazda Protoge traveling north on Burgin Parkway. About 20 minutes later, officers located the vehicle at a gas station and confirmed its stolen status through a CJIS Web check. The vehicle was running with a lone occupant inside.
During a search, officers found a wallet in the vehicle containing multiple credit and debit cards belonging to a citizen not associated with the vehicle owner, who had reported fraudulent charges earlier that day. The victim had lost his wallet after parking at an MBTA garage before attending a Celtics game and later received alerts of unauthorized transactions. The victim was able to retrieve his wallet from the station.
Further investigation revealed that the vehicle had been stolen from the Alewife parking garage in Cambridge on December 19, 2025. The operator was arrested.
This incident highlights the effectiveness of ALPR technology in aiding the recovery of stolen vehicles and personal property, as well as preventing further fraudulent activity.

quincy-ma-pd-:
On August 26, 2025, an officer responded to a report of a possible restraining order violation. The victim claimed that on the night of August 24, her vehicle had been vandalized when the front passenger tire was slashed. She suspected her ex-boyfriend, although she did not directly witness the incident and could not confirm it was him.
To investigate the allegation, the officers reviewed the Quincy Automatic License Plate Readers to track the ex-boyfriend's vehicle, a Jeep Cherokee. The readers revealed that the vehicle was not in Quincy during the time frame of the alleged incident, which was from 9:00 PM on August 24 to 7:45 AM on August 25. This crucial information showed that the ex-boyfriend's vehicle was not in the area, effectively clearing him of any involvement in the crime.
The use of Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPRs) helped confirm the ex-boyfriend's alibi, protecting him from a wrongful accusation and demonstrating the power of technology in providing accurate, unbiased evidence in criminal investigations. The cameras allowed law enforcement to quickly verify the movements of the suspect, preventing an unjust outcome for someone who might have otherwise been wrongly implicated.

quincy-ma-pd-:
The use of Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) technology has boosted hit-and-run clearance rates to 40% for the Quincy Police Department, far surpassing the national average of 10%. This technology allows for quick identification of suspects and key evidence, greatly improving the resolution of these cases. A recent hit-and-run investigation highlights how ALPR has helped solve incidents that might have otherwise gone unresolved.
In the case, Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPRs) and the Flock Camera system played a key role in solving this hit-and-run accident. A suspect vehiclelater identified as a blue 2018 Toyota Camrywas reported to have struck a delivery truck in Quincy and fled the scene. Initially, the suspect vehicle was linked to an individual, but after further investigation, discrepancies began to emerge.
The victim, the driver of the damaged delivery truck, identified the vehicle by make (Toyota Camry). However, upon further interviews and investigation, it became clear that the vehicle involved in the incident was not the Toyota Camry, but rather a silver Hyundai Elantra with a similar license plate. The Flock Camera system provided crucial evidence, capturing images of the Hyundai Elantra with front-end damage, further supporting the victim's account and revealing the true vehicle involved in the accident.
Through the ALPRs, the officer identified the Hyundai turning away from the scene around the time of the incident. A search of the license plate data revealed a vehicle registered to an individual living in Quincy. After multiple attempts to locate the vehicle and the driver, the officer eventually made contact with the owner, who admitted to being involved in the accident but initially panicked and fled the scene.
This case highlights how the Flock Camera system, through its license plate tracking and vehicle recognition capabilities, helped investigators identify the correct vehicle, dispelling earlier assumptions and confirming the true details of the hit-and-run. The technology was instrumental in clearing up the case and ensuring the right individual was held accountable for the accident.

column1: What Is Flock Safety?
mill-creek-wa-pd:
Camera network: Flock Safety installs and maintains a network of ALPR cameras throughout the City of Mill Creek.

Data collection: Cameras capture license plate information, which is sent to an encrypted cloud storage with an established retention period.

Integration with law enforcement: License plate data is then shared with existing law enforcement databases, such as the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), to detect current Law Enforcement Status (stolen vehicles, stolen plates, warrants, or missing persons).

Crime solving: By providing a database of license plate information, the ALPR system helps police solve crimes faster by identifying vehicles with associated Law Enforcement Status.

column1: What Flock Safety is Not
mill-creek-wa-pd:
A traffic enforcement tool: The cameras are not traffic cameras, do not detect speeding, and cannot issue tickets for traffic infractions.

A facial recognition system: The technology does not have facial recognition capabilities and does not capture biometric information.

An immigration enforcement tool: Per the Mill Creek Police Department Policy and Data Sharing Agreement, the system is not to be utilized for immigration enforcement (see Prohibited use).

An unlimited law enforcement data source: The system has network authorizations which allow agencies the ability to allow or prevent sharing with Federal, State, or local agencies (see Organizations granted access to MCPD data).

Suspect was arrested by Barton County, MO deputies. This suspect and vehicle were associated with multiple cases and the suspect had multiple felony warrants from multiple jurisdictions.

8. FLOCK alert for a vehicle with an individual with an active Warrant. The suspect was also a suspect regarding the violation of a protection order. Officers located the vehicle in the area of the FLOCK alert. Suspect was located inside of the residence of the protected party of the PFA. Suspect was arrested.

9. FLOCK alert on a stolen vehicle, vehicle was located in an apartment complex parking lot. The vehicle fled the area southbound out of the city and failed to navigate a turn and wrecked the stolen vehicle. Suspects fled on foot and were not apprehended. Investigation ongoing.

City of Saratoga Success Stories
santa-clara-county-ca-so:
July 2022: A Saratoga resident reported people entering their backyard and stealing patio furniture. Although the residents surveillance camera captured images of the vehicle used to steal the patio furniture, the incident occurred at night and the camera was unable to detect the vehicles license plate number. A nearby ALPR camera was able to detect the vehicles license plate at night and this information provided an investigative lead that allowed the Sheriffs Office to identify one of the suspects responsible for the theft.

September 2022: A call was reported to the Sheriffs Office that a group of suspects followed a Saratoga resident from a retail store to the victim's residence, entered the open garage of the victim's residence where the victim was unloading groceries from his vehicle. One of the suspects then pointed a firearm at the victim, demanded the victim's Rolex watch and cash from the victim's wallet, to which the victim complied. The victim gave a good description of the vehicle. Using that information, the known time frame of the crime, and the ALPR system, deputies were able to share identifying information with other law enforcement organizations and the suspect was ultimately arrested by a partner agency.

October 2022: Deputies received an ALPR hit in Saratoga for a stolen vehicle. The vehicle was located and stopped. In addition to possession of a stolen vehicle, the driver also had an outstanding warrant for prowling and was arrested. The vehicle was returned to the registered owner.

November 2022: Deputies received an ALPR hit for a vehicle associated with felony crimes in Saratoga. The vehicle was located, deputies attempted to stop the vehicle, but the suspect driver did not yield and recklessly evaded until running out of gas on State Route 85, where the suspect was taken into custody.

January 2023: Deputies received an ALPR hit for a stolen vehicle in Saratoga. The vehicle was located a short time later, and deputies attempted an enforcement stop, but the suspect driver did not yield and recklessly evaded. The suspect's vehicle eventually became disabled and the suspect was detained without further incident. The suspect admitted to knowing the vehicle was stolen and also had an outstanding warrant for auto theft and was driving without a license. The suspect was arrested.

column1: FLOCK SAFETY CAMERA POLICY
skamania-co-wa-so:
The Skamania County Sheriff's Office authorizes the use of FLOCK SAFETY cameras for law
enforcement and community safety purposes. These devices gather and analyze the data to
enable the rapid identification and location of vehicles and persons of legitimate interest to law
enforcement. The FLOCK SAFETY camera used by the Skamania County Sheriff's Office to
convert data associated with vehicle license plates for official law enforcement purposes, including
identifying stolen or wanted vehicles, stolen license plates, Amber Alerts, Silver Alerts, and
Missing/Endangered Persons.

The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the use, management, and operation
of FLOCK SAFETY cameras by the Skamania County Sheriff's Office. The Skamania County
Sheriff's Office is committed to utilizing FLOCK SAFETY cameras to enhance community safety,
deter and solve crimes, maintain public trust, and support the overall mission of the Skamania
County Sheriff's Office.

Southern Shores Police Department ALPR History
southern-shores-nc-pd: Southern Shores, NC Police Department has been using ALPRs since early 2019. Leonardo ELSAG ALPRs to be specific. The department started with 7 ALPR cameras, the main purpose at the time was to use these to obtain more accurate vehicle/traffic counts of vehicles related to the highly sensitive concerns of cut through traffic. They were located on some of the main thoroughfares (cut through) streets in town. While the focus at the time was vehicle counts, the ALPRs also assisted this department in numerous criminal investigations that resulted in both apprehension of criminals and recovering of stolen vehicles and endangered/missing persons. In 2025 we purchased Flock Safety ALPRs to replace many of the outdated ELSAG ALPRs, we also added additional ALPRs to better secure the town of Southern Shores to better protect our residents and their properties.

STERLING HEIGHTS POLICE DEPARTMENT
GENERAL ORDER


GENERAL ORDER NUMBER: 6.81
SUBJECT: AUTOMATED LICENSE PLATE READERS (ALPR)
DATE OF ISSUE: 11/25/2025
EFFECTIVE DATE: 11/25/2025
RESCINDS: 03/19/2025

POLICY

It is the policy of the Sterling Heights Police Department to utilize ALPR technology to capture and store digital license plate data and images while recognizing the established privacy rights of the public. The data and images gathered provide information and investigative resources to employees. The use and access of such systems and information shall be for law enforcement purposes only and in compliance with all applicable training, policies, procedures, rules, regulations, and laws.

PURPOSE

This purpose of this policy is to establish a minimum set of binding guidelines to govern the use of Automated License Plate Reader to include data collection, management and use of LPR data, and maintenance of LPR equipment.

AUTHORITY

Sterling Heights Police Department Manual of Rules, Articles I, II, and VI. Title 18 of the United States Code Chapter 123.2721 - Prohibition on release and use of certain personal information from State motor vehicle records.

DEFINITIONS

Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) System equipment consisting of cameras, computers, and computer software used to automatically recognize and interpret the characters on motor vehicle license plates. Digital images captured by the cameras are converted into data which is processed through the ALPR system.

Hot List A list of license plates associated with vehicles of interest compiled from one or more databases including, but not limited to: National Crime Information Center (NCIC), Michigan Secretary of State, local BOLOs, etc.

Vehicles of Interest Vehicles including, but not limited to, vehicles which are reported as stolen, display stolen plates or tags, are linked to missing and/or wanted persons, and vehicles flagged by the Secretary of State or other Law Enforcement agencies.

Hit An alert from the ALPR system that a scanned license plate number may be in the NCIC or other law enforcement database for a specific reason such as, but not limited to: stolen car, wanted and/or missing person, terrorist related activity, and AMBER alerts.

ALPR Administrator The Chiefs designee(s), serves as the ALPR Administrator for the department.

PROCEDURES

Training:

No member of the Sterling Heights Police Department shall access ALPR data without first completing department approved training.

ALPR Administrator shall be responsible for planning and implementing all department approved training concerning the ALPR.

Automated License Plate Reader Confidentiality:

Use of the ALPR system, software, associated databases, and data is restricted exclusively to the Departments law enforcement functions. Information obtained from the ALPR, software, associated databases, and data shall not be used for personal reasons or for reasons inconsistent with the Departments law enforcement functions under any circumstances.

Misuse or abuse of the ALPR system, software, associated databases, or data may be subject to criminal prosecution, civil liability, and/or administrative sanctions, up to and including termination, pursuant to and consistent with the relevant collective bargaining agreements and Department policies.

Information obtained from the ALPR system, software, associated databases, and data shall not be disseminated to the public except as authorized by law.

Information obtained from the ALPR system, software, associated databases, and data may be disseminated to other law enforcement agencies or officers when it is to be used for law enforcement related functions, providing all of the following criteria are met:

The law enforcement agency makes an official written request for the ALPR data through LEIN or via department email.
The agencys identity, the person requesting the data, and the intended purpose must be documented in such a manner as to demonstrate compliance with this policy and retained on file with the vendors software.
A supervisor must approve the request.

Automated License Plate Reader Use:

The ALPR system, software, associated databases, and data may be used in conjunction with any routine patrol operation or criminal investigation. Reasonable suspicion or probable cause is not required before using an ALPR.

Officers shall be aware the ALPR system will not have access to real time data. Hot lists, NCIC, LEIN, etc. are updated on a regular basis, but not continually, therefore there may be a delay in entries and removals.

Upon receiving an alert, officers should verify the plate and the state of issuance match the hot list alert in the ALPR system.

Officers should then conduct a check of the plate in question in LEIN/NCIC to verify the entry.

Upon locating the vehicle officers shall visually verify that the license plate on the vehicle matches that of the image captured by the ALPR and the LEIN/NCIC check before proceeding with any investigative or enforcement action.

Officers are reminded that an alert alone shall not be the basis for police action. For example, if a vehicle is entered into the system because of its association with a wanted individual, Officers should attempt to visually match the driver to the description of the wanted subject prior to making the stop or should have another legal basis for making the stop.

Restrictions of Automated License Plate Reader Use:

The ALPR system shall only be used for official and legitimate law enforcement purposes. Only sworn police personnel and dispatchers shall have access to the ALPR system.

The ALPR system shall not be used for the sole purpose of immigration
enforcement.

Invasion of Privacy: Except when done pursuant to a court order such as a search warrant, it is a violation of this policy to utilize the ALPR to record license plates on private property. The exception is license plates on private property that are exposed to public view.

Harassment or Intimidation: It is a violation of this policy to use the ALPR system to harass and/or intimidate any individual or group.

Personal Use: It is a violation of this policy to use the ALPR system for any personal purpose.

RESPONSIBILITY

Automated License Plate Reader Administration:

The Chief of Police or designee is responsible for administrative oversight of the ALPR system operations and shall be responsible for the following:

Ensuring access, collection, secure storage, and retention of ALPR data and associated media files are within policy guidelines.
Ensuring ALPR reads and alerts or hits that are acted upon in the field or associated with arrests, investigations, and/or prosecutions are documented in the vendors database.
Ensuring that ALPR system audits are conducted on an annual basis. System audits shall be designed to ensure the integrity of data captured, stored, and/or retained and shall include a review of password security and system usage.
Ensuring that each employee who uses or has access to the ALPR system has completed department approved training and is certified to have access to the Law Enforcement Information Network (LEIN).

ALPR system repairs (hardware or software) shall be made by the current ALPR system vendor or a vendor approved by the Chief of Police.


Data Retention and Accountability:

1. All ALPR data will be stored on the current Vendors server for a period of thirty (30) days. After thirty days the data shall be purged unless it has become, or it is reasonable to believe it will become, evidence in a criminal or civil action or is subject to a lawful action or order to produce records. In such circumstances, the applicable data shall be transferred to another digital media and stored according to current procedures.

2. All saved data shall be closely safeguarded and protected by both procedural and technological means. The Department will observe the following safeguards regarding access to and use of stored data:

a. All requests for access to historical ALPR data shall be logged in the ALPR system and the reason for the access must be recorded. The appropriate Sterling Heights Police Department case or incident number shall be documented in the request.
b. All ALPR data downloaded to a mobile workstation shall be accessible only through a login/password protected system capable of documenting all access of information by name, date, and time.

Administrative Audits:

1. It is the responsibility of the Chief of Police to ensure that an audit is conducted of ALPR detection browsing inquires at least once during each calendar year. The Sterling Heights Police Department will audit a sampling of the ALPR system utilization from the prior twelve (12) month period to verify proper use in accordance with this General Order. The audit shall randomly select at least ten (10) detection browsing inquiries conducted by Sterling Heights Police Department employees during the time period selected to determine if each meets the requirements of this General Order.

The audit shall be performed and documented by the ALPR Administrator in the form of a Memorandum to the Chief of Police. The memorandum shall include any data errors found so that such errors can be corrected. After review by the Chief of Police, the memorandum any associated documentation shall be filed in accordance with current Michigan State Police record retention policy.

Damage to ALPR Camera:

If an officer is dispatched to or locates a damaged ALPR camera, they shall write a case report or note it on a UD-10.

An Evidence Technician shall respond to take photographs of the damaged pole and/or camera.

The current vendor, FLOCK, requests the damaged pole and/or camera to be left closest to the location it was originally placed.

The OO shall notify the Captain of Administration via email of the damaged pole and/or camera and provide the case number.

The Captain of Administration or their designee shall notify FLOCK via email (support@flocksafety.com) or by phone (866-901-1781) and work with City Hall to have the pole and/or camera replaced.





_________________________
Andrew Satterfield
Chief of Police

column1: Burglary Spree Solved
tompkins-county-ny-so:
Tompkins County, NY - January 5, 2026

Since November 3, 2025, the Tompkins County Sheriff's Office has investigated a series of storage facility burglaries across Tompkins County. Investigators utilized Flock Safety technology to assist in developing a vehicle description linked to the incidents.

On February 5, 2026, during surveillance, investigators observed a male subject inside a storage unit with a cut lock that did not belong to him. Through investigative leads, including information developed with the assistance of Flock Safety, Jarrod C. Nickerson, age 36, of Lansing, NY, was identified and apprehended.

Nickerson was charged with Burglary in the 3rd Degree (Class D felony) and remanded to the Tompkins County Jail on $20,000 cash bail following arraignment in CAP Court. A subsequent search warrant executed on February 6, 2026, with assistance from the New York State Police Bureau of Criminal Investigation, resulted in the recovery of stolen and suspected stolen property.

Approximately 25 individuals or families are believed to have been impacted across multiple counties. Investigators continue working to identify property owners, and additional charges are anticipated.

These are allegations only. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

column1: Stolen Vehicle Located & Fugitive Apprehended
tompkins-county-ny-so:
City of Ithaca, NY - December 31, 2025

A Tompkins County Sheriff's deputy received a Flock Safety alert regarding a stolen motor vehicle from Broome County near Green and Cayuga Streets. A deputy located the vehicle on Ithaca Road and conducted a traffic stop. The driver was charged, and the passenger was held on an active warrant from North Carolina until extradition could be arranged.

column1: Smash and Grab Larceny Suspects Identified
tompkins-county-ny-so:
Town of Groton, NY - October 2, 2025

Deputies identified two suspects involved in 7 local smash-and-grab larcenies from vehicles, who were also involved in similar incidents in Broome, Chenango, Delaware, and Otsego Counties. Credit cards, bank checks, and personal identification were stolen to commit various acts of fraud. Both have active warrants out of multiple states, some with nationwide extradition. The investigation continues.

column1: Alleged Homicide Suspect Identified and Located
tompkins-county-ny-so:
Dryden, NY - October 8, 2025

Tompkins County deputies assisted a neighboring county with identifying and locating a homicide suspect who, after allegedly committing the crime, fled to his home in the Town of Dryden in Tompkins County.

column1: Apprehension of Stolen Vehicle & Stabbing Suspect
tompkins-county-ny-so:
On September 23, 2025, at approximately 8:00 p.m., a Tompkins County Sheriff's Deputy, while assigned to a joint Gun Involved Violence Elimination (GIVE) detail received a Flock Safety alert of a stolen Chevrolet Silverado out of Rochester, NY entering the City of Ithaca.

Deputies and Ithaca Police Officers located the vehicle in the parking lot of a restaurant on Elmira Road in the City of Ithaca. When law enforcement activated their emergency lights and ordered the driver to exit, the suspect attempted to flee by reversing the truck but was blocked in by other vehicles. He then fled on foot but was quickly apprehended.

Further investigation revealed that the suspect had an active felony warrant from the Monroe County Sheriff's Office and pending charges from the Rochester Police Department related to his alleged involvement in the stabbing of two victims earlier that day.

column1: Missing Cortland Man Safely Located by Tompkins County Deputies with Assistance from Flock Safety Technology
tompkins-county-ny-so:
Lansing, NY - September 1, 2025

At approximately 9:13 AM, Tompkins County Sheriff's Deputies were alerted by Flock Safety Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) cameras that a vehicle connected to a missing person case from Cortland County had just been detected in North Lansing.

The vehicle had been entered into the Flock system during the previous shift by the on-duty TCSO Sergeant, as the Sheriff's Office was assisting the Cortland County Sheriff's Office in locating the missing 92-year-old male.

Deputies quickly intercepted the vehicle and conducted a stop in the parking lot of the Mirabito Gas Station at 32 Peruville Road, Lansing. They confirmed that the driver was indeed the missing Cortland man, who appeared confused and stated he had been driving all night in an attempt to return home.

Deputies coordinated with the Cortland County Sheriff's Office to ensure the safe return of the man to his residence in Cortland.

"This case highlights how technology, when paired with strong collaboration between agencies, can bring about safe and successful outcomes," said Sheriff Derek Osborne.

column1: Success Story 1
wilton-ct-pd: On March 29, 2025, the Wilton Police Department received a report of public indecency involving a male subject who had allegedly exposed himself to two juvenile victims. The victims provided a description of the suspect's vehicle, which was searched in Flocks database, yielding a match. Shortly thereafter, a neighboring police department responded to a similar report involving the same suspect vehicle, in which the operator allegedly exposed himself to a juvenile within their jurisdiction. With the objective evidence obtained from Flock the offender was identified and subsequently charged with Risk of Injury to a Child, Breach of Peace in the Second Degree, and Public Indecency.

column1: Success Story 2
wilton-ct-pd: On May 15, 2025, the Wilton Police Department received a report of an elderly female resident who had failed to return home. A search of the Flock database revealed that her vehicle had recently been observed in New York State. The individual had no known reason for traveling to that location, and her family determined that the trip likely occurred during an episode of mental confusion. She was formally reported as missing, and local New York law enforcement were advised of the missing individual but could not locate her. The vehicle's registration was added to a Flock hotlist. Several hours later, on May 16, 2025, at approximately 12:25 a.m., Flock notified officers that the vehicle was actively traveling within the Town of Wilton. Responding personnel located the vehicle and successfully reunited the individual with her family.

column1: Success Story 3
wilton-ct-pd: Multiple area police departments were experiencing a crime pattern of organized retail theft. Through collaborative investigations, law enforcement identified a suspect vehicle and entered its registration into a Flock hotlist. On June 21, 2025, the Wilton Police Department received a Flock alert indicating that the suspect vehicle had entered the town. Officers initiated a search of local shopping centers and located the vehicle parked in the lot of a grocery store. While engaging the vehicle's operator, a second individual emerged from the store pushing a shopping cart with merchandise. Upon observing the officers, the second individual attempted to depart the scene. Further investigation revealed that the operator and the second individual were traveling together. The merchandise in the cart was confirmed to have been shoplifted from the store. Additionally, during the course of the investigation, fentanyl was discovered inside the vehicle. In summary, the Flock Safety alert enabled officers to locate the suspect vehicle, identify its occupants, and interrupt a larceny in progress.

column1: Success Story 4
wilton-ct-pd: On July 16, 2025, Flock LPR cameras in the Town of Wilton alerted officers to a vehicle traveling through the area, whose registered owner was the subject of an active arrest warrant for domestic violence. Utilizing the vehicle details provided by Flock, officers located the vehicle and took the subject into custody without incident.

column1: Recent Success Story's
woodland-ca-pd:
January 2025
CHP Kidnapping Suspects Arrested- Incident 25007035
On January 16, 2025, at approximately 1638 hours, the California Highway Patrol let law enforcement agencies in Woodland know they were tracking a kidnapping suspect via a phone ping and they were headed into Woodland. The suspect vehicle, a white Acura, was captured on a Flock License plate Reader (LPR) camera at County Road 98 and W. Kentucky Ave. as it entered Woodland, and Woodland PD officers checked the area for the suspect. The suspect vehicle was soon located by CHP on County Road 102 at Maxwell Ave., and it was involved in a traffic collision with an uninvolved vehicle after a brief vehicle pursuit as law enforcement
attempted to stop the vehicle. The two suspects fled on foot from the Acura, but were quickly apprehended.

February 2025
Stolen Vehicle Suspect Fled to Southern California- Case WDP25-000445
On February 3, 2025, at approximately 0817 hours, a Woodland PD officer was dispatched to the 300 block of W. Main St. for a stolen vehicle report. The victim advised she parked her Ford in her apartment parking lot a few days prior and just noticed it missing. The officer checked the Flock system and noticed the Ford was captured on a camera in Moreno Valley a couple hours before taking this report. The Ford was entered into the Stolen Vehicle System.

Suicidal Person Located/Saved  Incident #25022031
On February 20. 2025, officers received information through dispatch of a suicidal person reported to the Yolo County Sheriffs Department. The license plate was provided in the informational be on the lookout incident shared to Woodland PD. A Woodland officer used the Flock camera system to check for the vehicle and saw that it had entered Woodland at 0210 hours in the area of County Road 98 and Main Street. He later located the vehicle a few blocks away. Several officers responded to the area, located the subject, and applied life saving measures and administered Narcan. Their proactive use of Flock and quick actions resulted in the individuals life being saved.

July 2025
Stolen GMC from Lincoln, CA- Case WDP25-002725
On July 9, 2025, at approximately 2343 hours, Woodland PD officers received an alert on their department phones that a stolen GMC was just captured on a Flock LPR camera on East St. at Sports Park Dr. It was quickly determined the GMC was stolen out of Lincoln, CA, and the identity of the suspect was known. The suspect, a 36-year-old Woodland resident, also had a confirmed felony warrant out of Placer County. Officers located the GMC at Walmart (1250 E. Gibson Rd.), and the known suspect was contacted nearby. The suspect initially provided a false name, but his real identity was confirmed and he was arrested on multiple charges including the
vehicle theft, the warrant, impersonating another person while committing a felony, and possession of drug paraphernalia.

August 2025
College St. and Main St. Shooting- Case WDP25-003327
On August 16, 2025, at approximately 0011 hours, officers responded to the area of Main St. and College St. regarding multiple gunshots heard outside the Stag Bar. Bullet casings were located, shattered glass from a nearby business was determined to be caused by bullets, and witnesses were interviewed. After video surveillance was obtained from a business, the suspect vehicle was found to be a Chevrolet Equinox with some unique characteristics. Officers checked the Flock LPR cameras nearby, and located a Chevrolet that matched the suspect vehicle description around the time of the shooting. Officers searched the city for the Chevrolet with this license plate, located it, and found it matched the unique identifiers as seen in the initial video surveillance. A search warrant was served at the Chevrolet owner's residence. The suspect, a 25-year-old Woodland resident was arrested and multiple firearms were located. Once this first suspect was arrested, officers wrote search warrants into his social media. With this information, a second shooting suspect was eventually identified, who was a 24-year-old Woodland resident. A search warrant for his residence was served, he was arrested, and multiple firearms were located.

February 2026
On February 12, 2026, officers responded to a residence in Woodland regarding a disturbance involving a mother and her estranged teenage daughter. The mother arrived at the home and attempted to take property from the daughter. A physical altercation followed, during which the mother assaulted the daughter. The daughter sustained injuries and was later treated at a local emergency room. During the incident, the mothers boyfriend attempted to flee the scene in a vehicle while the
daughter was partially hanging out of it. Based on the circumstances, a felony child abuse want was established for the driver. Officers conducted follow-up efforts over the next two weeks to locate the suspects and the vehicle but were initially unsuccessful. The investigating officer entered the suspect vehicle into he FLOCK mobile application. On February 26, the officer received an alert indicating the vehicle was entering Woodland. Officers responded to the area, located the vehicle and both
suspects, and took them into custody without incident.

column1: Yuba County SO - Facebook Post - LPR Fact versus Fiction
yuba-county-ca-so:
A technology that helped identify and arrest a homicide suspect within hours! Flock LPRs: lets talk about the facts  and clear up the fiction. Ever since Flock Safety license plate reader cameras were installed throughout Yuba County in November 2022, theyve helped deputies solve case after case. Stolen vehicles recovered. Suspects identified. Crimes connected. Real investigations, real victims, real results. But along with good technology comes some creative storytelling. So, let's clear a few things up. The cameras do NOT identify drivers or passengers : They do NOT spy on what youre doing inside your vehicle: They do NOT record your road trip playlist: They are NOT used to issue speeding tickets or other traffic violations: They DO capture license plates and vehicle details to help law enforcement investigate crimes: They DO provide time-stamped data that helps connect cases and locate suspect vehicles: They DO help us keep our community safer. Think of them like a really smart notebook that remember vehicles, not people. We get it. New technology can feel a little Big Brother-ish. But if youre worried about being tracked everywhere you go& your cell phone would like a word. The goal here is simple: protect our community using tools that help deputies solve crimes faster and more efficiently, while respecting privacy and staying within the law.
